2868.description: When people with SUD/OUD want help after hours, their options are limited to checking themselves into ED or calling 911 to request a Marchman Act. These are the most expensive entry points into the behavioral health system of care and are often inappropriate. Recovery Epicenter Foundation (REF) has established the Catcher's Mitt as an affordable/effective/immediate alternative solution. They offer 24/7 admission by certified recovery peer specialists who help clients to build their recovery capital and then navigate them into an appropriate longer-term program. Additionally, REF houses clients of treatment programs who have a recurrence during their treatment program. Instead of these programs releasing individuals to an unsafe or unsober home (or to the street), REF will provide housing for them until they have the requisite abstinence time to return to their treatment program. This pro
2868.purpose: Goal: Reduce number of overdose deaths, 911 calls, and ED hospital admissions. By: Bridging ~9 day gap between desire to get into treatment/recovery and enrollment in a program which will increase retention in recovery. By: Reducing days between unsuccessful completion of treatment due to recurrence and return to treatment program through admission to respite recovery. By: Reducing the number of people released to the streets -- either upon successful completion of treatment or upon unsuccessful
2868.activities: Provide 24/7 respite recovery housing to 350-400 people with OUD/SUD for an average of 9 days. Increase participants recovery capital (which is a validated measurement of recovery that best aligns with DSM V) and navigate participants to appropriate longer-term treatment/recovery programs. 90% of participants will matriculate to a longer treatment/recovery program. 90% of participants will demonstrate an increase in recovery capital.
2868.direct_services: Provide 24/7 respite recovery housing to 350-400 people with OUD/SUD for an average of 9 days. Increase participants recovery capital (which is a validated measurement of recovery that best aligns with DSM V) and navigate participants to appropriate longer-term treatment/recovery programs.

2868.outcome: Outcomes: 1. significant improvement in connection to care for those early in recovery journey in comparison to those without 24x7 access to safe/sober housing 2. 97% of individuals will matriculate from respite housing to recovery/treatment program. 3. significant decrease in length of time to return to recovery/treatment programs after recurrence 4. increase recovery capita for those involved in program Measurements 1. Utilize participant tracking system and partner verification (employer and apprenticeship placement data); third-party evaluation report.

1102.description: This project will construct and improve sidewalks in critical areas to enhance pedestrian safety and accessibility, particularly for school children and residents with mobility challenges. The improvements will bring sidewalks into compliance with ADA standards, reduce pedestrian accidents, and provide safer routes to schools, public facilities, and community spaces. The project supports long-term public safety, promotes walkability, and ensures equitable access for all residents, including the elderly and physically disabled.
1102.purpose: The requested funds will construct approximately 10,000–12,000 linear feet of sidewalks around AC-Perry K-8 in Miramar to improve pedestrian safety for students and neighborhood residents. The project will provide safe walking routes to school, reduce the need for children to walk in roadways, and support the City’s Complete Streets and redevelopment initiatives in Historic Miramar.
1102.activities: Construction of approximately 10,000–12,000 linear feet of new sidewalks, including grading, concrete pouring, ADA- compliant curb ramps, crosswalk striping, and installation of pedestrian signage to ensure safe school and neighborhood access.
1102.direct_services: The project will provide safe, ADA-compliant pedestrian pathways, reducing the need for children and residents to walk in roadways, thereby improving safety, accessibility, and walkability within the community.
1102.population: The project will primarily serve students at AC-Perry K–8 and nearby neighborhood residents. Approximately 1,200 students and more than 3,000 local residents are expected to directly benefit from improved pedestrian safety and access.
1102.outcome: Expected benefits include reduced pedestrian accidents, safer routes to school, and increased neighborhood walkability. Outcomes will be measured through City of Miramar Public Works monitoring, school safety audits, and resident feedback surveys.

1077.description: The Town desires to install safety guardrails between the road and the canal bank along Hancock Road (SW 142 Avenue) from State Road 848 (Stirling Road) to Old Sheridan Street. The proximity of this road to the canal has led to serious injuries and tragic results on several occasions.
1077.purpose: The intent of this project is to increase safety along this roadway and to save lives. On numerous occasions, the proximity of the canal has led to serious injuries as it is simply too easy for vehicles to run off the road and into the canal due to the lack of guardrail or other approved barrier.
1077.activities: Guardrail will be installed along Hancock Road (SW 142 Avenue) from State Road 848 (Stirling Road) to Old Sheridan Street to increase safety along this roadway and to save lives.
1077.direct_services: Business recruitment, job creation and related economic opportunities will be enhanced for the State, and its adjacent municipalities, by providing a safer corridor. This construction project will employ nearly 40 Floridians within the next year, including surveyors, engineers, inspectors, and construction workers.
1077.population: Hancock Road connects State Road 818 to State Road 848 (Stirling Road) to Old Sheridan Street. The installation of guardrail along Hancock Road will dramatically increase the safety of the thousands of motorists that traverse it each day, allowing the traveling public to conduct business with local merchants and companies that directly access this roadway.
1077.outcome: The intent of this project is to increase safety along this roadway and to save lives. This will be measured by the number of accidents on the roadway.

1104.description: The Rolling Oaks neighborhood has only one entrance and exit: SW 178th Avenue. This roadway is prone to flooding, which creates emergency hazards for the approximately 350 homes in the neighborhood. When the only roadway into the neighborhood is under water, it delays response times for emergency services thereby placing lives at risk. The Stormwater Master Plan recommends adding a drainage trunkline along approximately 1,000 linear feet of SW 178th Avenue. The proposed project includes the conveyance, trunkline and outfall pipes with 21 proposed structures.
1104.purpose: The project goal is to provide flood relief and improved water quality to all constituents. This project is part of the Town’s overall resiliency efforts to create a healthy community while improving water quality. This project will remove flood waters from roads in this heavily traveled area. It will provide critical drainage capacity for storm-water runoff, thereby reducing roadway flooding (both volume and duration), and the frequency of property damage and personal injury.
1104.activities: The Stormwater Master Plan recommends adding a drainage trunkline along SW 178th Ave between SW 52nd Court and the canal at SW 178th Ave (approximately 1,000 linear feet). The proposed project includes the conveyance, trunkline and outfall pipes with 21 proposed structures. All existing swales are to be regraded. Concrete aprons on both existing and proposed drains are to be renewed or designed to mitigate the surrounding landscaped area’s impedance of roadway runoff flow.
1104.direct_services: The Rolling Oaks neighborhood has only one entrance and exit: SW 178th Ave. This roadway is prone to flooding, which creates emergency hazards for the approximately 350 homes in the neighborhood. The project will remove flood waters from the roadway. It will provide critical drainage capacity for storm-water runoff, thereby reducing roadway flooding and the frequency of property damage and persona
1104.population: The execution of this project will provide flood relief to all of constituents. It is a highly traveled area that serves as an emergency access route during evacuations and other emergency purposes.
1104.outcome: The purpose of this project is multi-faceted, with one objective set to reduce stormwater staging in the basin and the other to significantly increase water quality. The outcomes will be measured through water quality testing and basin capacity reports.

1726.organization: Youth and Family Alternatives, Inc. dba Youth
1726.description: Provides funding to continue construction of The Center which will house the following local organizations: Youth and Family Alternatives dba Youth and Family Advocates (YFA) child welfare program, the community-based care lead agency staff and their subcontracted diversion provider, the Department of Children and Families Child Protective Investigation services, respite beds, and other non-profit agencies serving children and families in the local community. The purpose of the Center is to have services for children and families under one roof, providing the opportunity to collaborate and centralize services and obtain optimal outcomes for families. This centralization of services will also allow for the stabilization and controlling of lease expenses in addition to the reduction of service disruptions, which often occurs due to rising lease expenses and leases not being renewed due to
1726.purpose: Funds will be used to build The Center for Children and Families, which will serve as a family-centered community resource to support families involved in the child welfare system. Through coordinated services, the Center aims to strengthen families, promote child safety, and reduce the time children spend in foster care. The Center will provide a family-centered hub, co-location of child welfare programs to include YFA case management and adoption services, Florida DCF Child Protective Services
1726.activities: The Center will house and co-locate the full continuum of Child Welfare Programs in Pasco County. Co-location and collaboration between providers will result in earlier family engagement, meaningful visitation, service referral and prompt linkages to provide child safety and family strengthening. Co-location will also reduce current expenditures on leases by DCF, Community Based Care lead agencies, YFA, Diversion providers and those funds can be reinvested in services for children and families a
1726.direct_services: The Center will: • Serve as Community Hub for family centered child welfare services. • Provide a central location to ensure families have access to meaningful visits with their children, access to case plan services, and streamline communication with case workers and service providers. • Co-locate YFA’s case management, adoptions, and visitation program; Department of Children and Families Child
1726.population: The Center will serve children and families involved in the child welfare system in Pasco County. It is anticipated based on the current number of families served, that more than 800 children and their families will be served annually.
1726.outcome: The Center will house and co-locate the full continuum of Child Welfare Programs in Pasco County. Co-location and collaboration between providers will result in earlier family engagement, service referral and deployment intended to provide child safety and family strengthening. Co-location will also reduce current expenditures on leases by DCF, Community Based Care lead agencies, YFA, Diversion providers and those funds can be reinvested in services for children and families and the non-profit programs. The methodology will be the percentage of families diverted from the dependency system at the time of service delivery and within 6 months of case closure. Also, the percentage of children in

1137.description: A 158,291 sq. ft. medical/clinical facility located on FIU Campus in western Miami-Dade County. Facility will provide direct healthcare services to the community through a partnership with an affiliated local hospital system. This location will provide and enhance interdisciplinary health science education (Medicine, Nursing, Social Work, Public Health, and more) as well as health science research for all components of the FIU Academic Health Sciences Center.
1137.purpose: Medical services will include primary care, surgical, medical specialties including orthopedics, oncology, and cardiology. All services will be provided in an interdisciplinary model engaging with complete integration of services for patients, as well as student educational experiences.
1137.activities: All services will be provided in an interdisciplinary model engaging with complete integration of services for patients, as well as student educational experiences.
1137.direct_services: Direct services will include medical services to patients and will serve as an entry to a large regional and comprehensive health sciences platform.
1137.population: The elderly, persons with poor mental health, persons with poor physical health, economically disadvantaged persons, developmentally disabled, physically disabled, students in preschool, grade school, high school, university, and college. It will serve thousands of people on a yearly basis.
1137.outcome: The academic health center will be modeled on an existing platform which provides centralized and well-orchestrated health care delivery for a wide range of diseases. The center will have an acute care services area as well as ambulatory surgery and multidisciplinary array of services. FIU HWCOM faculty group practice will grow to add new services and expand deliverables on mental health support for our patients. HWCOM is already partnering with advanced technology companies to deliver first-to-market trans cranial magnetic treatment for mental health conditions and this service would be expanded.

2938.description: For the past 50 years, NEFBA has offered a quality, registered-apprenticeship program to provide career development in the skilled trades as a pathway to high-wage, high-demand careers in the construction industry. Employers, who sponsor apprentices through our Program, pay the apprentice's tuition over the course of the four years and the apprentices complete with zero debt and are averaging salaries of $62,000 per year. Funding from this project will support capital expenses to equip classrooms and training labs in the new NEFBA Workforce Education Center. This center is essential to meeting the growing regional demand for a highly skilled workforce, exemplified by a 12% increase in apprentices since our last appropriation request. Currently, we serve 542 apprentices across four trades, with plans to expand capacity to 600 apprentices by 2028.
2938.purpose: For the past 50 years, NEFBA has offered a quality, registered-apprenticeship program to provide career development in the skilled trades as a pathway to high-wage, high-demand careers in the construction industry. Employers, who sponsor apprentices through our Program, pay the apprentice's tuition over the course of the four years and the apprentices complete with zero debt and are averaging salaries of $62,000 per year. Funding from this project will support capital expenses to equip classroom
2938.activities: NEFBA offers an apprenticeship program to provide career development in the skilled trades as a pathway to high- wage, high-demand careers in the construction industry. NEFBA began the program in 1973 in response to the growing need for skilled craft workers in the local area. Currently, NEFBA offers Apprenticeship training in the fields of Carpentry, Electrical, HVAC and Plumbing. NEFBA's Apprenticeship Program is currently at capacity of 542 active apprentices, and this project will allow us t
2938.direct_services: The tuition-free NEFBA program provides great opportunities to those who are not college-bound, and leaves graduates with $0 in student loan debt with post-graduation wages of $62,000 or more. Upon graduation, apprentices are awarded up to 27 credit hours towards an A.S. degree in Industrial Management from the Florida state college system.
2938.population: Jobless persons, economically disadvantaged persons, at-risk youth, high school students, university/college students, formerly incarcerated persons, and veterans.
2938.outcome: This expansion of the Apprenticeship Program will provide increased opportunities for career development in the skilled trades as a pathway to high-wage, high-demand careers in the construction industry. Apprenticeship is the cornerstone of NEFBA's active workforce development services for the 5th largest homebuilders association in the nation. All registered apprentices are employed throughout the duration of their program by over 200 local employers. The tuition-free NEFBA program leaves graduates with $0 in student loan debt. Upon graduation, apprentices are awarded up to 27 credit hours towards an A.S. degree in Industrial Management from the Florida state college system through FSCJ. Th

1138.description: The Center for Creative Education's goal is to eliminate elementary illiteracy through creativity and the arts. Several years ago, CCE opened The Foundations School, an innovative, independent elementary school, which serves many of the poorest areas in Palm Beach County, at little to no cost to the families which attend. 100% of third grade students at The Foundations School that have attended since kindergarten are reading at grade level. This compared to a statewide average of 57%, and in the high poverty communities served by The Foundations School, only 34% of third grade students can read. Illiteracy is a pipeline to prison, homelessness, unemployment, and multi-generational poverty -- CCE is breaking that barrier through transformative approaches. Critically, literacy is the foundational pillar for all future learning. The need to admit more students to this unique, school choice
1138.purpose: The requested funds will enable the Center for Creative Education (CCE) and The Foundations School to expand space needed to add more students who are struggling academically and living in poverty. With a transformative education through creativity and the arts, our students are thriving; 100% of our third grade students that have been with us since kindergarten are reading on or above grade level. The need is overwhelming for this unique, independent school choice experience.
1138.activities: The goal of The Foundations School is enroll the maximum number of students to increase the positive impact on the community. CCE's current classroom space is fully committed. The new building will allow The Foundations School to double its capacity and expand its offerings to students on its four acre campus in West Palm Beach.
1138.direct_services: Students and families currently enrolled in The Foundations School will utilize the new space for art, STEM education (science, technology, engineering and math), and media arts education, as well as gallery space for student exhibits and performances. In addition, the facility will be available for the Center for Creative Education's many Palm Beach County-wide after school programs. The completi
1138.population: CCE and The Foundations School serve students who are behind academically, living in poverty, and are zoned to attend public schools in northern Palm Beach County which are chronically poor performers on state standardized tests. Once this building project is complete, The Foundations School will double in size to serve 180 students and 360 family members. CCE currently serves an additional 200 students enrolled in after school programs, and 400 family members, as well as 2,000 donors and commun
1138.outcome: The Center for Creative Education is at the forefront of educational innovation, reform, and school choice. We understand that every child is unique and not all students learn by the same methods of teaching. At the Foundations School, individualized assessments therefore drive instruction. Our goal is that 90% of all students attending our school will continue to perform at grade level or above in reading, math, and science. CCE provides services to after school students, and there are opportunities to engage the wider community with student projects (art galleries, films, shows, etc...).

1727.organization: Youth and Family Alternatives, Inc. dba Youth
1727.description: Speer II will expand the inventory of affordable housing in Pasco County for underserved populations. Speer I was constructed in 2019 and is a six-unit apartment building offering supportive housing to eight adults with developmental disabilities. Speer II will be located on the same property and will provide 50 newly constructed units of affordable housing, serving up to 110 families, children, and youth aging out of foster care. Rent will meet HUD Fair Market rent standards.
1727.purpose: Speer II, Affordable and Supportive Housing will provide 50 affordable housing units to serve up to 110 families, children, and youth aging out of foster care — helping to prevent homelessness and create pathways for long-term success in Pasco County. Speer II provides truly affordable housing, with 100% of the units within the Fair Market Rent for 60% AMI or below. Units will be designated to low- and very low-income families, youth aging out of foster care, and families reunifying through the
1727.activities: - Expand the inventory of safe, affordable, and accessible housing in Pasco County. - Provide 50 new housing units for up to 110 low and very low-income individuals, families reunified in the foster care system, and children aging out of the foster care system. - Offer affordable, newly constructed housing that is centrally located near or accessible to community resources, schools and health care. - The Pasco County Housing Authority offers 15 project-based vouchers assigned to the project. - P
1727.direct_services: Speer II will offer affordable, safe, and accessible housing for individuals and families that cannot afford current rent and housing costs and are at risk of homelessness. Units will be designated to low- and very low-income families, youth aging out of foster care, and families reunifying through the foster care system — groups whose primary barrier to stability is access to affordable housing.
1727.population: Speer II will potentially house any of the following: elderly, persons with poor mental and/or physical health, jobless persons, economically disadvantaged persons, at-risk youth, homeless, developmentally or physically disabled persons, pre and grade school students, university/college students, victims of crime, former foster youth that have aged out of foster care and are high risk for homelessness, and reunified families that were separated by foster care due to lack of housing.
1727.outcome: Affordable housing will provide safe shelter and stability for individuals and families. This will be measured by the number of families and individuals served and the percentage of occupied units.

1139.description: This project constructs a critical public access route to Key Biscayne’s beachfront, serving residents and visitors while protecting the island’s vulnerable dune system and endangered sea turtle nesting habitat. By guiding foot traffic along a controlled path, it prevents ecological damage and meets a mandatory requirement for the Village to rejoin the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Coastal Storm Risk Management Program—unlocking access to substantial federal coastal protection resources. The pathway also enhances public safety through a secure gated entry with after-hours locking and integrated camera surveillance, supporting emergency response and reducing liability risks.
1139.purpose: The requested funds will be used to construct a designated public access pathway to Key Biscayne’s beachfront that protects sensitive dune ecosystems and endangered sea turtle nesting habitats while ensuring safe, controlled access for residents and visitors. The project also fulfills a mandatory requirement for the Village to rejoin the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Coastal Storm Risk Management Program, restoring eligibility for significant federal coastal protection funding.
1139.activities: The project includes the construction of a secure, environmentally sensitive access path designed to channel pedestrian traffic and prevent ecological damage to the dune system. It also provides for installation of a gated entry with after-hours locking and integrated surveillance cameras, improving both public safety and resource protection.
1139.direct_services: Residents and visitors will benefit from a safe, accessible route to the beachfront that balances public use with environmental conservation. The project also enhances safety through controlled access, supports emergency response capabilities, and safeguards public spaces from after-hours incidents and liability risks.
1139.population: The project serves the entire Key Biscayne community as well as visitors to the island’s beachfront. While no specific number of individuals is provided, all residents and guests who access the beach will directly benefit from improved safety, accessibility, and environmental protection.
1139.outcome: The project is expected to result in a completed, environmentally compliant public access path that meets federal program requirements, protects the dune and sea turtle nesting habitats, and enhances safety for beachgoers. Outcomes will be measured by successful construction of the access route, compliance with environmental protection standards, requalification for participation in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers program and observed reduction in habitat degradation or after-hours incidents.

1155.description: The project addresses the root cause of shoreline recession, which threatens over $5 billion in property, critical infrastructure like electrical substations, and the Village’s only evacuation route. By reducing the frequency and cost of beach renourishments, the reef system offers long-term resilience against sea-level rise and storm surge. The structures are self-growing and self-repairing, adapting to environmental changes while enhancing biodiversity. This phase includes site assessment, preliminary design, and a permitting feasibility analysis to evaluate effectiveness and environmental impact.
1155.purpose: The requested funds will support the preliminary design of a submerged offshore reef system intended to protect Key Biscayne’s shoreline from erosion while preserving marine habitats. The goal is to develop a sustainable, nature-based solution that addresses the root causes of shoreline recession and enhances the island’s long-term resilience to sea- level rise and storm surge.
1155.activities: This phase of the project includes conducting a site assessment, developing a preliminary design for the reef structures, and performing a permitting feasibility analysis. These activities will evaluate the system’s effectiveness in reducing erosion, its environmental impact, and its potential as a long-term alternative to traditional beach renourishment methods.
1155.direct_services: While this phase focuses on design and assessment, residents will ultimately benefit from the future implementation of the reef system, which will provide shoreline protection, reduce flooding and erosion risks, and preserve local beaches. The project supports public safety, property protection, and environmental quality for the community as a whole.
1155.population: The project serves the entire Village of Key Biscayne community by protecting its coastline, which safeguards over $5 billion in property, vital infrastructure such as electrical substations, and the island’s only evacuation route. The population size is not specified, but all residents and businesses within the Village will directly or indirectly benefit.
1155.outcome: Expected outcomes include the development of a technically sound, environmentally sustainable reef design that demonstrates feasibility for shoreline protection and habitat enhancement. Success will be measured through completion of the site assessment, design deliverables, and permitting feasibility analysis, as well as documentation of projected erosion reduction and ecological benefits based on modeling and environmental studies.

1091.description: The FIU Category 6 WOW helps to research and test the ability of structures, components, products, and techniques to withstand the effects of (a) 195-200 mph winds, (b) surge, wave, and flooding associated with those extreme events, and (c) hurricane-spawned tornadoes. Findings will help policy makers to enhance preparedness and disaster management and implement code plus designs.
1091.purpose: For Florida to protect its economy and maintain its cutting-edge position in university-based hurricane research, innovation, and testing, the highly successful FIU Wall of Wind (WOW) hurricane simulator needs a complementary and more powerful testing facility capable of reaching 195-200 mph wind speeds, together with storm surge, wave, and flood testing capabilities.
1091.activities: FIU Wall of Wind for Category 6 will research and test the ability of structures, components, products, and techniques to withstand the effects of a Category 6 hurricane or stronger including (a) 195-200 mph winds, (b) surge, wave, and flooding associated with those extreme events, and (c) hurricane-spawned tornadoes.
1091.direct_services: There is a critical need for full-scale research and testing facilities capable of simulating extreme conditions and devising test solutions for stronger and safer communities. The research and testing from the facility will enhance preparedness, mitigation, and recovery.
1091.population: Any Floridian impacted by hurricanes or storm surge. This would serve the millions of citizens living in Florida.
1091.outcome: Reduction of economic losses and fatalities from natural disasters including hurricanes. Post-hurricane assessment to measure reduction in fatalities and insurance claims data for estimating reduction of economic losses. The Florida Public Hurricane Loss Model (FPHLM) can also measure the loss reduction using mitigation techniques

1068.organization: Living Skills in the Schools Inc.
1068.description: This project expands delivery of evidence-informed, school-based substance use prevention education in the School District of Palm Beach County, supporting compliance with Florida Statute 1003.42, which requires five hours of annual resiliency instruction addressing prevention of alcohol, nicotine, and drug abuse. As an approved district provider, the program offers classroom and assembly-style instruction led by licensed mental health professionals who teach students skills to resist peer pressure, make healthy choices, and strengthen resiliency. Instruction aligns with DOE’s Comprehensive Health Education and Resiliency Standards and integrates into the district’s behavioral health framework. Funding will expand services from 87 to 95 schools and increase presentations from 2,231 to 2,500 in the school year of 26/27, achieving a 5% increase in duplicated student reach and advancing sta
1068.purpose: The requested funds will support the School District of Palm Beach County’s implementation of Florida Statute 1003.42, requiring five hours of annual resiliency instruction including preventing alcohol, nicotine, and drug abuse. As an approved alternative provider, we deliver evidence-informed prevention programming that builds resiliency, supports healthy decision-making, and strengthens district capacity to meet DOE standards.
1068.activities: Funds will expand evidence-informed substance use prevention education in Palm Beach County schools, increasing reach from 87 to 95 schools and presentations from 2,231 to 2,500. Licensed professionals will deliver classroom and group instruction, raising duplicated student reach by about 5%, to over 82,208 students and school staff.
1068.direct_services: Students in Palm Beach County public schools will receive direct substance use prevention education through classroom and assembly-style presentations led by licensed mental health professionals. Sessions focus on preventing alcohol, nicotine, and drug use while building resiliency and healthy coping skills.
1068.population: The target population includes students in Palm Beach County public schools across elementary, middle, and high school levels. The program delivers school-based substance use prevention education that strengthens resiliency and decision-making. For the 2026–2027 school year, services will expand from 87 to 95 schools, providing over 2,500 presentations and reaching more than 82,208 students annually through classroom and assembly-style instruction.
1068.outcome: Funding will expand prevention education to 95 schools and over 2,500 presentations, increasing duplicated student reach by about 5%. Students will demonstrate improved knowledge of substance use risks, stronger refusal and coping skills, and greater overall resiliency, supporting safer, healthier school communities. Outcomes will be measured through pre- and post-program student surveys assessing knowledge, attitudes, and refusal skills related to substance use. Additional metrics include number of schools served, presentations delivered, and percentage increase in student reach to evaluate impact and program effectiveness.

1460.description: This project would include the replacement of manually-read water meters with remotely-read smart water meters. This project is to attempt to move the City of Bristol to utilize a more modern and efficient way of collecting water meter readings. This will reduce the manpower required to manually read meters and will allow the small City staff to spend more time on maintenance issues. Furthermore, the new meter technology can assist with the detection of leaks quicker which can reduce water losses for both the City and residents.
1460.purpose: These remotely-read meters will reduce man hours required in the field for meter reading so staff can spend more time on maintenance of the water system. The meter technology under this proposal provides continuous customer data and allows for early detection of water leaks/loss. The system will also provide the city with operational detail such peak flows for each customer. The system will also reduce revenue loss from inaccurate metering.
1460.activities: Design and construction of remotely-read meter system to help the City reduce costs associated with water leaks. Project will also help the City conserve water by assisting with early identification of leaks. The increased efficiency in meter reading will allow for the limited City staff to prioritize efforts on system maintenance and improvements.
1460.direct_services: New meters will be provided to all citizens connected to the Bristol public water system. As a result of these improvements the accuracy of the meters will be improved and early leak detection will be provided. This will allow the City to accurately bill the customers for true water usage while reducing the losses down stream of the meters.
1460.population: This project will benefit the entire City of Bristol, approximately 915 individuals.
1460.outcome: The proposed project will allow the City of Bristol to more closely monitor water usages and reduce the amount of unaccounted for water losses. Early leak detection will allow the City to reduce unnecessary groundwater withdraws. The City provides reports to the WMD regarding water losses. The volume of unaccounted for losses is expected to decrease as a result of this project.

1295.description: This capital project will provide supportive employment through the creation of a training kitchen. The intent is to provide a job training ground for clients in mental health/substance use treatment who are nearing a phase in recovery allowing for community reintegration. It will provide work skills preventing cycles of chronic unemployment, jail and homelessness. It will lower tax payer costs, reduce jail and crisis recidivism and over utilization of emergency services and law enforcement.
1295.purpose: This project will improve the infrastructure of the kitchen for the Lightshare crisis emergency campus (Baker Act and Marchman Act receiving facility) to provide supportive employment. The intent of these supportive employment services is to provide a training ground for people currently in stable mental health and substance use treatment recovery. These clients need skills to work preventing them from entering cycles of chronic unemployment, and wages that may not support appropriate housing.
1295.activities: The facility enhancement will assist in provide skills to gain employment, live independently, and deliver ongoing support services through case management and other mental health and substance use disorder services There is value added to the community as it provides inclusion, competitive employment, impacting effects of other social determinants of health such as homelessness, joblessness, mental health instability. The facility provides services to help clients gain reasonable rates of pay,
1295.direct_services: The facility is a bridge for support services for current and future employment needs. The program will build and extend support with local agencies and partners to assist in maintaining employment, which provides stability for the client and the workplace. It will provide ongoing support services through case management, through medication assisted treatment programs, walk-in center services resi
1295.population: Persons in Sarasota County who suffer from mental health and substance use disorders; individuals experiencing a behavioral health crisis. It is anticipated the program will serve 2500 individuals per year.
1295.outcome: Practical hands-on assistance will be provided to help people handle the necessity of daily living and assist them in the recovery process. The program is designed to offer opportunities to help clients who are motivated to develop career driven talent and enter the local workforce. Vocational skills will help them live independently, gain employment, and deliver ongoing support services through case management and other mental health and substance use disorder services The intent of these services is to provide a supportive employment training ground for people currently in stable mental health and substance use treatment recovery. These clients need skills to work preventing them from ente

2473.description: Learning Independence for Tomorrow Inc. (LiFT) is a private, nonprofit organization specializing in the education of K-12 students and adult learners with neurodiversity. The LiFT University Transition Program (ages 18-22+) and the Adult Training Program (serving adults 23 and older) provide integrated academics, essential life skills training (how to cook, take public transportation, grocery shop and balance finances), and career pathways designed to help students gain and keep employment. State funding to renovate and activate unused space on campus will enable LiFT to launch a comprehensive Family Resource Center that will provide coordinated access to educational services, therapy and behavioral health, primary and specialty healthcare navigation, legal consultation, and financial counseling to families and students enrolled in LiFT Academy, LiFT University, and the LiFT Adult Traini
2473.purpose: Funds will renovate and equip unused space to create the LiFT Family Resource Center, a centralized, fully accessible hub on LiFT’s campus that connects neurodivergent individuals and their families to coordinated services including therapy, healthcare, behavioral, legal, educational services, and financial supports. By centralizing intake and case-navigation, the center will reduce the time, cost, and complexity borne by families in locating and qualifying for services especially those raising
2473.activities: The renovated campus hub will offer a comprehensive range of coordinated activities and services supporting neurodivergent individuals and their families at every stage of life. It will provide access to speech, occupational, and behavioral therapy, as well as health and wellness navigation through local medical partnerships. Families will receive legal and financial guidance, including guardianship, benefits, and long-term planning, plus educational assessments, transition planning, and lifelon
2473.direct_services: The center will provide walk-in and scheduled support, individualized case navigation, referrals, and counseling to neurodiverse students, adults, and families. Services will include direct assistance accessing benefits, healthcare, employment pathways, legal and financial resources, and education supports, improving independence, family stability, and long-term quality of life.
2473.population: The project is expected to serve over 1,191 individuals. It will primarily serve children, teens, and adults with neurodiversity, including individuals with autism, Down syndrome, ADHD, and other learning or intellectual differences. It will also support families and caregivers, including parents, siblings, and guardians who often face challenges navigating fragmented service systems and accessing consistent support. In addition, the broader community will benefit through partnerships with local
2473.outcome: The outcome of this project will be a fully integrated, centralized hub that improves access to essential services and enhances the quality of life for neurodivergent individuals and their families in Pinellas County. By bringing therapeutic, educational, vocational, legal, and financial supports together in one location, the project will eliminate barriers created by fragmented systems and ensure consistent, person-centered care. This coordinated approach will lead to measurable improvements in independence, employability, and community inclusion. Beyond the individuals directly served, the project will strengthen family stability, foster collaboration among local service providers, and cre

2044.description: Building on FIU's academic excellence and deep community ties, the Global Jewish studies program will connect local and global Jewish experiences while preparing students for leadership in education, public service, diplomacy, and cultural preservation. It will position FIU—and Florida—as national leaders in advancing Jewish Studies, celebrating Jewish culture and heritage, and combatting hate.
2044.purpose: Funds supporting activities enhancing educational quality and promoting anti-hate awareness, Jewish Studies course development and research on Israel and antisemitism, teacher trainings, and student fellowships; hosting public lectures and cultural events; and delivering community workshops that increase understanding of Jewish history and culture while equipping citizens to counter bias and hate.
2044.activities: Track the number of public lectures, cultural events, exhibits, and K–12 outreach experiences offered annually, alongside attendance figures, audience composition, and participant diversity. Document growth in engagement with Jewish history, culture, and antisemitism and Israel awareness across FIU and throughout Florida.
2044.direct_services: The Center will provide a wide range of direct services, including access to public lectures, cultural events, and exhibitions; K–12 teacher training and classroom outreach; development of new courses and academic programs; community workshops addressing antisemitism; and creation of fellowships, internships, and policy-relevant research opportunities for students and scholars.
2044.population: University students and the general population.
2044.outcome: Track the number of faculty and staff positions, postdoctoral fellows, graduate assistants, interns, and affiliated educators directly and indirectly supported by the Center. Monitor career development opportunities created through funded positions, mentorship, and research grants.

2447.description: To provide the funding needed to create two Disaster Resilience Staging Sites for rural communities of western Flagler County. The sites would be paved and elevated to reduce the risk of flooding, and utilized to stage emergency resources, distribute food / water, and provide other disaster services. The site will serve as an investment and resource to the state emergency management apparatus for future storms and disasters. Staging and distribution of emergency supplies (food, water, tarps, etc) Staging and deployment of emergency and infrastructure repair vehicles and staging and operations of sanitary stations (showers, restrooms, laundry, etc).
2447.purpose: To provide the funding needed to create two Disaster Resilience Staging Sites for rural communities of western Flagler County. The sites would be paved and elevated to reduce the risk of flooding, and utilized to stage emergency resources, distribute food / water, and provide other disaster services. The site will serve as an investment and resource to the state emergency management apparatus for future storms and disasters.
2447.activities: These sites would be created by elevating and paving areas on existing County properties and adjacent to existing paved roads. Mobilization, site work, and surveying would be completed by Flagler County as in-kind services. These sites would support the provision of critical emergency and post-disaster (hurricanes, wildfires, floods, etc.) services.
2447.direct_services: All services associated with the needs after a disaster which could also include physical and mental health support and services, as well as any informational resources. Staging and distribution of emergency supplies (food, water, tarps, etc) Staging and deployment of emergency and infrastructure repair vehicles Staging and operations of sanitary stations (showers, restrooms, laundry, etc).
2447.population: These sites will be open to the general public and accessible to any resident with an estimated service population of 140k. However, these sites will be located in the underserved area of Flagler County and will have a specific target population of residents from Bunnell and other rural areas located in Western Flagler.
2447.outcome: Staging sites can be used as a hub for health services and psychological support to individuals experiencing trauma from the disaster. They can offer useful resources, information and support for individuals in their long-term recovery. It will also reduce the impact of disasters, allow for the public to recover more quickly, strengthen local economies, and create safer places to live. This leads to a quicker return to self-sufficiency and vitality after a disaster and attracting new businesses and residents. Effectiveness of the sites will be measured through statistics of usage, positive health outcomes, number of resources utilized and number of residents and local businesses indicating q

2454.description: Funds will support construction and engineering construction administration costs to extend approximately 2,080 linear feet of 8-inch gravity sewer to connect unserved properties near Lake Stella. The project will improve water quality by reducing nutrient loading to groundwater and Lake Stella within the Lower St. Johns River Main Stem BMAP area, while expanding the City’s customer base to increase utility revenue.
2454.purpose: The project will extend centralized sewer service along Cherry Street near Lake Stella. This will reduce nutrient loading to groundwater and nearby surface waters, improve water quality, and expand the City’s wastewater customer base, strengthening both environmental protection and economic sustainability.
2454.activities: Funds will support bidding, construction, and construction inspection/administration for approximately 2,080 linear feet of 8-inch gravity sewer, installation of 11 new sewer service connections and associated water services, manhole connection, testing, and site restoration.
2454.direct_services: Residents will receive direct access to the City’s centralized wastewater system, eliminating the need for individual septic systems. This improves public health, protects water quality, and provides reliable sewer service for connected homes.
2454.population: The project directly benefits approximately 11 residential properties along Cherry Street and indirectly benefits the broader Crescent City community of roughly 1,700 residents by improving water quality and utility reliability.
2454.outcome: Expected outcomes include reduced nutrient loading to Lake Stella, improved groundwater and surface water quality, and expanded wastewater service capacity. These benefits will be measured by the number of septic tanks decommissioned, new customer connections completed, and nutrient reduction estimates documented through BMAP compliance reporting and DEP project closeout documentation.

2456.description: The Appropriation will provide the remaining construction funds needed to complete the North Tower and Lake Argenta Water Main Improvements project. Work includes replacing and extending water mains along key corridors to improve fire flow, water pressure, and service reliability. This funding will bridge the gap from the initial FY 2025-26 appropriation, ensuring the full project is completed to enhance system performance, resiliency, and future growth capacity.
2456.purpose: The funds will complete the remaining construction activities for the North Tower and Lake Argenta Water Main Improvements, increasing fire flow capacity, water pressure, and overall reliability of Crescent City’s potable water system. Phase 2 will extend and interconnect critical water mains to improve water delivery to residents and businesses and strengthen the City’s ability to meet current and future demands efficiently and safely.
2456.activities: The City will proceed with bidding, award, and construction of the remaining water main extensions and replacements along key corridors. Work will include installation of new PVC mains, valves, fittings, and fire hydrants, as well as service connections, testing, and restoration. Engineering services during construction will ensure compliance with plans and specifications, successful pressure and flow testing, and certification of improvements.
2456.direct_services: The project will directly improve service reliability and water quality for residents and businesses by reducing main breaks, improving pressure consistency, and ensuring adequate fire flow for emergency response. These upgrades will protect public health and safety, support property protection, and improve water system performance for the entire community.
2456.population: The project will serve approximately 1,700 residents, as well as local schools, businesses, and critical facilities within Crescent City. All customers connected to the City’s potable water distribution system will benefit from improved water pressure, fire protection, and system reliability.
2456.outcome: The project will result in measurable increases in water pressure and fire flow capacity, improved service reliability, and reduced water loss. These benefits will be verified through pre- and post-construction flow and pressure testing, system monitoring, and maintenance reports confirming improved operational performance and reduced service disruptions.

1105.description: Allapattah Community Action (ACAI) Inc. is a private not for profit organization 501 (c) (3) chartered by the State of Florida in May of 1978 to provide services to the needy elderly residents Miami Dade County. The elderly are served meals in a congregate setting at our center once a day, five days week. Over 350 seniors are served meals five times a week. Through our home delivery system we also serve homebound clients. Daily age appropriate social, recreational and educational activities are also held at the center, tailored to the culturally diverse backgrounds of each program participant. Examples of such activities include nutritional educational counseling, field trips and outings to promote socialization, and bingo/other games held at our facility.
1105.purpose: The purpose of the requested funds is to continue providing meals, transportation and recreational activities to our elderly low-income clients.
1105.activities: We will provide meals, and activities like bingo and dominoes for our clients, as well as arts and crafts, computer literacy courses, and transportation.
1105.direct_services: Direct services include serving 9135 meals to 35 congregate clients and homebound (via delivery) setting to 39 clients 10,296 meals to as well as transportation of 70 clients to different recreational and cultural outings 5,171 trips, and group activities like bingo and dominoes, art, etc. to 60 clients for 1,843 activities in the physical community center.
1105.population: Elderly clients, over the age of 60 who are low-income and extremely low-income. The number of individuals expected to be served are 35 clients for congregate meals, 39 for Homebound Meals delivered by our catering company, 70 clients who utilize transportation services to access the center and 60 clients for recreational activities.
1105.outcome: ACAI documents and maintains intakes and assessment in each client file together with all screening information, services provided information and referral and follow-up. All information is reviewed and assessed for client demographics, services received, information and referrals and all follow-up activities. Staff tracks client intake and assessments, information and referral, achievement of goals and objectives, client services and activities, document units of services, program activities, generates standard reports, closes client cases, generates monthly reports, client satisfaction surveys, achievement/outcomes, and tracks overall client improvement.

2458.description: Funds will support critical upgrades to the City’s Water Treatment Plant, including pumping systems upgrades, process controls, and elevated storage tank modifications. The project will replace aging and deteriorated components to enhance reliability and efficiency. Modern controls will improve pressure management and optimize performance while lowering maintenance costs and strengthening long-term system sustainability.
2458.purpose: The project will improve the reliability, efficiency, and safety of the City’s potable water system through critical upgrades to the Water Treatment Plant’s pumping systems, process controls, and elevated storage tank. These improvements will modernize aging infrastructure and operational sustainability.
2458.activities: The project will include design, permitting, bidding, construction, and construction administration/inspection services for WTP improvements. Work will consist of replacing and upgrading pumping and electrical systems, installing new process controls and monitoring equipment, and completing modifications to the elevated storage tank to enhance system efficiency and performance.
2458.direct_services: The project will ensure reliable, safe drinking water service to residents, businesses, and community facilities. Improved system controls and monitoring will provide consistent water pressure and quality, reduce service disruptions, and conserve resources, directly benefiting customers and protecting public health.
2458.population: The project will directly serve Crescent City’s approximately 1,700 residents and all customers connected to the municipal water system, including local businesses, schools, and critical facilities. The benefits extend to visitors and surrounding communities that rely on Crescent City’s water infrastructure for regional stability and growth.
2458.outcome: The project will enhance system reliability, improve water quality, and reduce operational costs. Success will be measured by decreased maintenance incidents, reduced non-revenue water losses, improved water pressure and flow consistency, and compliance with FDEP water quality standards verified through sampling, monitoring, and operational performance records.

2459.description: Putnam County is seeking an appropriation for a new ERP financial system. Putnam County’s current financial software system is an antiquated and obsolete DOS based system (AS400) which provides significant challenges. The new financial software system would provide Putnam County Board of Commissioners and the Putnam County Clerk of Court and Comptroller increased productivity, improved data security and accuracy, and improved customer service to both internal users as well as the citizens we serve.
2459.purpose: The purpose of the funds will be to purchase and implement a new comprehensive solution for Putnam County's Enterprise Financial Software System. Putnam County's current system is DOS based, its severely limited in functionality and security. The current system is expected to be at end of life and support for system is expected to be unavailable sometime during the next three years.
2459.activities: (1) A formal solicitation for the selection of a system, (2) engagement of a contractor to implement the new system and (3) recovery/transfer of old records from the current system
2459.direct_services: A new system would allow for greater transparency of governmental operations to the citizens of Putnam County. The system would streamline efficiencies for local vendors doing business for the government. This investment will provide improved services through automation along with data integrity and protection.
2459.population: The system will serve the entire community.
2459.outcome: A new system would provide greater customer service, availability of enhanced data metrics and increased transparency of government operations. This outcome will be measured with availability of increased data metrics, reports and real time information available to the citizens.

1230.organization: Southeastern Guide Dogs, Inc., DBA - Dogs,
1230.description: Dogs Inc is seeking funding to mitigate the effects of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and ease mobility challenges for veterans through the placement, training, and care of highly skilled working dogs, including guide, service, facility therapy, and skilled companion dogs. Support includes match personalized to needs of veteran, professional on- campus or in-home instruction, and follow up support: all at no cost to the recipient. Support will also benefit Gold Star families. Funding will help eliminate financial barriers, ensuring every veteran or Gold Star family in need can access the healing power of a loyal, life-changing dog.
1230.purpose: The specific goal is to reduce PTSD symptoms, ease mobility challenges, and strengthen mental and physical health: helping veterans reclaim independence and emotional stability. Funding will be used to provide trained guide, service or skilled companion dog specifically matched to needs of individual veterans, in-depth on-campus or in-home training for veteran-dog teams, lifetime follow up care and evaluations for each team, which includes dog food, monthly preventatives, and veterinary care.
1230.activities: Dogs Inc provides highly trained dogs specifically matched to needs of veterans; in-depth on-campus training for veterans, including lodging, meals and student educational materials or home placement when needed; follow-up care for each human–dog team, which includes dog food, monthly preventatives, annual veterinary care, and regular team evaluations for life of guide and service dog teams.
1230.direct_services: Dogs Inc pairs expertly trained dogs selected and prepared for each veteran’s unique needs, and offers immersive team training and lifelong support to ensure the team’s success. Providing a service dog to a veteran with PTSD can reduce the disorder’s negative effects on family life by lowering stress, irritability, and hypervigilance, improving relationships and household stability. As a result, f
1230.population: The target population to be served are veterans with vision loss, veterans suffering from PTSD and other disabilities, and Gold Star families. Estimated number to be served by our guide, service, skilled companion and facility therapy dogs based on current alumni and fiscal year goals is 5,500 individuals.
1230.outcome: The expected benefits of this project to veterans are improvement of physical and mental health. We measure success through regular outcome assessments tracking mobility, confidence, and independence. Alumni satisfaction is captured through surveys and direct feedback to ensure services remain responsive and effective. Testimonials underscore how our dogs transform lives: https://www.cnn.com/2025/09/18/us/video/colorado-veteran-service-dog-heroic-save-btc

2522.description: Upgrade the St John's Harbor Water System. Current system was non-compliant when transferred to the County via FDEP upon being abandoned by private ownership. Needed upgrades consist of reconstructing treatment ponds, replacing RO filters, hydropneumatic tanks, and groundwater storage tank. System will continue servicing the Bostwick community.
2522.purpose: Upgrade the St John's Harbor Water System. Current system was non-compliant when transferred to the County via FDEP upon being abandoned by private ownership. Needed upgrades consist of reconstructing treatment ponds, replacing RO filters, hydropneumatic tanks, and groundwater storage tank. System will continue servicing the Bostwick community.
2522.activities: Re-establish and bring the wastewater pond into FDEP compliance. Replace existing ground water storage tanks that are beyond their useful life. Replace outdated hydropneumatic tanks.
2522.direct_services: Sustainable and the ability to maintain potable water to FDEP standards.
2522.population: Citizens within the service district for St. John's Harbor water system.
2522.outcome: The funding would offset the project cost burden placed on consumers and allow for a reduction on the monthly maintenance cost. This outcome will be measured by lower utility bills to the citizens being served

2928.description: Hastings Main Street, Inc., seeks funding to relocate two historic structures, the FEC Carpenter's Shop and the St. Johns Electric Company Trolley Depot to the Hastings Main Street District. Funds will cover the move from the St. Augustine Airport to placement along the St. Augustine-Palatka Trail head and at the Old Jail site on Cochran Avenue in Hastings. These funds will also completely place the structures and cover the permitting, engineering, utility hookups, and getting a Certificate of Occupancy for both structures. These structures are targets of demolition if not relocated from their current site. Facilities will be restored for common public good and preservation of area history, and they offer a wonderful opportunity for the community to have a community/education center as well as facilities along our bike trail to achieve our Trail Town Designation. Property & structures wi
2928.purpose: The purpose of the funding serves to enhance historic preservation in Hastings. This rural agricultural community has deep roots linked to Flagler Era personalities and structures including the railroad. In the 1890s the community served as the agriculture supply to Flagler Hotels in St. Augustine and subsequently the nation. Funding for these structures allows for ongoing community education of the impact of food production and networks in supporting surrounding communities. We will be working
2928.activities: Hastings Main Street will arrange for movers, contractors, and ancillary help to move the two depots. The organization will subsequently renovate and restore the structures for public benefit as museums and community centers. Public access will encourage town revitalization and economic stability. Also, by creating incubator spaces in one of the buildings it will make the spaces self-supporting in providing income to sustain the properties so that they are never a burden to taxpayers.
2928.direct_services: Citizens of Hastings will gain educational insight into the railroad history and agricultural economy through ongoing interpretive stories, exhibits, and community public forums. Additionally, we will provide SBA & business training workshops for economic vitality and growth. We are working with the Council on Aging and our local schools on collaborative projects involving gardening and food prep,
2928.population: The immediate target population served is the residents of Hastings, which is in the process of revitalization. The Town of Hastings was dissolved in 2017 and suffered tremendous economic challenges over many decades. The historic depots will contribute to the revitalization of the economy and spirit of the community as it re-emerges as a thriving agri-tourism community. We are working on creating an inviting to community that gives pride to our locals but also attracts tourism for economic vita
2928.outcome: The benefit of adding historic structures with viable economic activity aids in adding to the area tax base through increased tourism. Hastings Main Street Inc., collects quarterly data on economic progress of its promotion and preservation activities. Increased jobs are anticipated as the larger structure will be retrofitted with small business incubator spaces to encourage and train small business development. Since Jan 2023 Hastings Main Street has contributed to investments over $14.5 million in public/private investments revitalizing the town.

2523.description: The City completed a pavilion shelter on city-owned lands in October of 2025. The space is currently used to serve meals by non-profit groups to those in need each night. Future development of this site includes construction of a community drop-in center, which when completed, will allow those in need to access additional services, including healthcare, dental care and social security benefits
2523.purpose: The community hub will provide space for non-profits and other organizations to service citizens in need.
2523.activities: Once constructed, space will be available for service providers to provide the various wrap around services to our community members in a centralized location. Services will include medical assessments, dental, mail, assistance with job searches, housing, food, and other services.
2523.direct_services: Access to health care, meals, referrals for services and transportation. The goal is to assist those members of the community who are experiencing homelessness and to prevent those on the verge of homelessness from ending up there.
2523.population: Approximately 75 people per week currently use "Dining with Dignity" and that number continues to grow. At a minimum, we expect the same number of community members to be served by a Drop-In Center.
2523.outcome: The expected benefit is to connect community members who are experiencing homelessness or on the verge of experiencing homelessness, with the services available to help them stay in their homes or move to a housed situation. Data will be continuously kept on the number of people served by the various service providers at the drop-in center.

2525.organization: St. Johns County Board of County
2525.description: This project increases the capacity, efficiency, and connectivity of CR 2209 from State Road 9B to County Road 208, by adding additional lanes, upgrading intersections, and extending the roadway from State Road 16 to County Road 208. The Central Segment of CR 2209, provides a state mandated north-south corridor parallel to I-95. The project is expected to improve traffic and pedestrian safety and is anticipated to alleviate traffic on I-95, a SIS facility.
2525.purpose: This project completes the Central Segment of CR 2209, providing north-south connectivity and enhanced traffic and pedestrian safety. Completion of CR 2209 is anticipated to alleviate traffic on I-95, a SIS facility. The project will feature bike paths, sidewalks, and a multi-use trail. In addition, this project will serve as a major transportation corridor for the planned K - 8 school to be completed in 2026 with a projected capacity of 1,500 students.
2525.activities: Programmed funds will alleviate traffic safety concerns and congestion in the County from State Road 9B to County Road 208. This has a direct benefit to the citizens of St. Johns County and those traveling through St. Johns County by improving the surface transportation system's level of service.
2525.direct_services: The direct service provided to citizens will be increased Level of Service (LOS) after improvements are completed along the CR 2209 from State Road 9B to County Road 208.
2525.population: This project will benefit not only the residents of St. Johns County (population 320,110), residents from surrounding counties, and the 10 million tourists who visit St. Augustine each year. In addition, this project will serve as a major transportation corridor for the the planned K - 8 school to be completed in 2026 with a projected capacity of 1,500 students.
2525.outcome: The improvements will increase traffic and pedestrian safety, reduce total lost time, and decrease congestion on I-95. CR 2209 connects the interior of St. Johns County with the future Florida East Coast Expressway. This will strengthen the transportation network within the county, providing access for new and existing businesses to regional a regional assets, such as JIA & JAXPORT. The outcome will be measured through annual traffic counts along the corridor and reduction of traffic incidents.

2526.organization: EPIC Community Services, Inc. dba EPIC
2526.description: Women seeking inpatient, residential treatment for their substance use disorder may wait up to 90 days for bed availability in our service area. Funding is requested to continue the 6 beds allocated for women-specific treatment services in our EPIC Recovery Center located in St. Johns County. These services offer intensive residential treatment for women living with significant substance use disorders or co-occurring mental health challenges. A specialized collaborative approach is used that includes individual, group and family therapy, psychiatric interventions, medication assisted treatment, care coordination, peer support and family reunification activities. This request is supported by the St. Johns County Board of County Commissioners, St. Johns County Behavioral Health Consortium, UF Health St. Johns, Betty Griffin Center (domestic violence provider) and the St. Johns County Famil
2526.purpose: The goal is to maintain access to Level 1 inpatient residential treatment services for women living with a substance use disorder by funding 6 beds at the EPIC Recovery Center in St. Johns County. This funding request will address the specific need for women's intensive, person-centered treatment services as identified by community providers of child welfare, domestic violence, and health care services. A core element of this initiative is ensuring that women can remain actively involved in thei
2526.activities: A specialized therapeutic modality will be implemented that addresses women-specific issues including trauma, grief and loss, self-esteem/body image, anger, familial relationships, and co-occurring mental health concerns of anxiety, depression and eating disorders. Our residents will also receive care coordination, peer support, life-skills coaching, parenting and recreational/art therapy.
2526.direct_services: Direct services will include a collaborative approach of therapists, nurses, psychiatric providers, care coordinators and peer specialist to offer intensive, short-term (30 day) residential treatment to build a solid foundation for recovery.
2526.population: Adult women with a substance use disorder with a priority given to pregnant women, women with children and women transitioning from incarceration. Approximately 100 or more women will be served.
2526.outcome: Reduce Substance Use. Measure: Reduction of symptoms. Completion of the treatment episode of care. Employment and safe housing achieved post discharge and reunification of women and their children. Method for measuring outcome: Adherence to patient’s treatment/recovery plan and care coordination plan that addresses substance use and/or mental health disorder treatment, employment, housing, benefits, primary healthcare, transportation, social connectedness, etc. Completion of St. Johns Family Intensive Treatment Team (FITT) program.

2527.description: Expansion of the firefighter training programs at First Coast Technical College to increase the number of certified graduates and address critical workforce shortages in St. Johns County and the surrounding region. The demand for qualified firefighters is growing rapidly due to accelerated retirement rates, expanding populations, and increasingly complex emergency response requirements. St. Johns County and its neighboring jurisdictions are experiencing persistent staffing shortages that place additional strain on existing fire crews and risk delayed emergency response times. To meet this challenge, First Coast Technical College seeks to expand its firefighter training capacity, enabling a greater number of certified responders to enter the workforce each year with the necessary credentials and readiness to serve.
2527.purpose: Funds will be used to purchase a fire pumper and renovate the existing drill tower, including adding additional classrooms to enhance safety and expand instructional capacity within the firefighter training program at First Coast Technical College. By maximizing utilization of existing facilities, equipment, and personnel, the funding will allow a program expansion and improve overall cost efficiency, support a measurable increase in student enrollment which will support local and regional fire
2527.activities: Purchase of a fire pump vehicle and renovation of drill tower, purchase of portables for additional classroom space & necessary equipment for the increased enrollment and meeting required safety standards. This will eliminate the current waiting list for the program by enabling a greater number of students to complete the state-required certification and enter the firefighting workforce.
2527.direct_services: The appropriation will directly support the expansion of firefighter training programs, eliminate the current waiting list for the program by enabling a greater number of students to complete the state-required certification and enter the firefighting workforce. As these graduates join local and regional fire departments, the availability of skilled first responders will increase, strengthening em
2527.population: The target population served by this project includes aspiring firefighters and emergency medical services (EMS) students from St. Johns County and the broader Northeast Florida region. These individuals are seeking the training and certification required to begin careers in the fire service and related emergency response fields. Through the expansion of its firefighter training program, First Coast Technical College anticipates serving an additional 60 to 80 students annually. These individuals
2527.outcome: The expected outcomes of this project are an increased number of certified firefighter graduates, enhanced training quality, and a stronger regional pipeline of qualified candidates ready to serve in fire departments across Northeast Florida. By expanding training capacity, the program will offer more realistic training scenarios, promote teamwork and leadership development, and better prepare students for the demands of the profession. Outcomes will be measured by increased enrollment, elimination of current waiting lists, and increase in the number ot certified graduates in the program.

1224.organization: Florida Association of Agencies Serving the
1224.description: Florida Agencies Serving the Blind, through its member agencies across the state, provides Expanded Core Curriculum (ECC) instruction for children ages 5-13 who are blind or visually impaired. This year-round program operates at member agency facilities and community sites across the state. The evidence-based ECC ensures academic success and delivers essential real-life experiences that prepare children for future employment beyond what public schools offer. By bringing children from entire counties together, the program also addresses the social isolation often experienced in school settings. Additionally, the ECC includes a critical parent component, offering support, advocacy, and practical solutions to child-rearing challenges, empowering families to help their children thrive.
1224.purpose: The program ensures that blind and visually impaired children gain the technical and personal skills necessary to thrive academically and socially alongside their sighted peers. Additionally, children acquire blindness-specific social, academic and pre-vocational skills through the expertise and collaboration of a dedicated team of professionals through local FASB member agencies tailored to the unique make-up of the children in the program.
1224.activities: Academic success skills--braille, large print; safe travel skills and white cane training; social interaction; recreation and healthy living; safe cooking, self-care and hygiene, managing money and budgeting, time management, assistive technology and screen readers, experiential introduction to careers; self-advocacy, making good choices, planning for adulthood; and sensory skills (hearing, touch, taste, smell, balance).
1224.direct_services: The program provides targeted, personalized instruction to blind and visually impaired children at local FASB member agency offices, in their homes, and at community sites to equip them with essential skills that address the unique challenges of blindness. The instruction focuses on helping children compensate for the effects of blindness on their academic achievement, social integration, and voca
1224.population: Children ages 5-13 who are blind or visually impaired in the State of Florida and their parents or primary caregivers.
1224.outcome: Academic achievement, acquisition of social and pre-vocational skills. Assessment through Pre- and Post- tests normed for blind/visually impaired children in academic, independent living, technology and other skills in the 9 Expanded Core Curriculum skills (See b. above).

2528.organization: St. Johns County Board of County
2528.description: This multi-stage project constructs the Florida Museum of Black History campus, which will serve as a nationally significant museum and performing arts center. The project will enhance the public's access to African American History, provide new opportunities for education and research, and further the cultural enrichment of Floridians and the many national and international patrons that will visit the museum. As statutorily required, the Florida Museum of Black History Task Force selected St. Johns County as the location for the statewide Museum of Black History.
