2326.description: The requested funds will retrofit and equip a facility on a UWCF campus to serve as a Step-Down Disaster Recovery Shelter. This project will allow schools to close emergency shelters and reopen faster, while offering residents the stability, case management, and resources needed to transition back into permanent housing and restore normalcy after disaster. The space could also serve as a disaster volunteer housing and staging area or point of distribution to get supplies out to the community.
2326.purpose: The requested funds will retrofit and equip a facility on a UWCF campus to serve as a Step-Down Disaster Recovery Shelter. This project will allow schools to close emergency shelters and reopen faster, while offering residents the stability, case management, and resources needed to transition back into permanent housing and restore normalcy after disaster. The space could also serve as a disaster volunteer housing and staging area or point of distribution to get supplies out to the community.
2326.activities: Funds will support facility upgrades to provide a step-down shelter on UWCF's campus, space for case management and recovery support services, or supply distributions post-storm. Activities will include retrofitting the building to meet shelter standards, installing a generator and refrigeration units, updating bathrooms and electrical systems, and ensuring accessibility and safety compliance.
2326.direct_services: The shelter will provide safe, temporary housing, meals, and access to essential recovery services, including case management, FEMA or insurance assistance, and mental health support. It will also serve as a hub for distributing recovery supplies, coordinating volunteers, and offering programs that strengthen community resiliency.
2326.population: The target population is anyone seeking shelter after a disaster has occurred and the school shelters need to close so that schools may re-open for business. This could include anyone in the general public. The target population outside of disaster will include community members who are supported by community resiliency programming provided by United Way of Central Florida and our nonprofit partner agencies. We anticipate serving more than 800 individuals through the shelter space on the United
2326.outcome: This project will enhance community resiliency, protect the general public, increase economic activity, and improve the quality of education. The UWCF campus will provide year-round space for us and partner organizations to offer programs across all impact areas, including preparedness events, trainings, and community education. The Step-Down Shelter will protect residents after disasters by providing a safe, supervised environment for displaced families and volunteers, preventing unsafe living conditions, and supporting recovery. Economic activity will also be stimulated through construction activity, new staffing needs, and expanded partner programming. Success will be measured through ind

1309.description: Disaster Recovery & Management - Global Empowerment Mission is fully committed to serving all Florida residents in the wake of any disaster. In 2024, GEM served over 1 million Florida residents after several disasters, most notably performing large-scale responses in the aftermath of both Hurricanes Helene & Milton. In 2025, GEM has carried out several hurricane preparedness distributions in Florida communities. GEM is also the official disaster-relief partner of Miami-Dade County and is counted on to rapidly respond to them.
1309.purpose: GEM's headquarters, located in Doral, Florida is fully-equipped to respond immediately to disasters, and with partners such as Good360, Amazon, Publix, & many others, GEM is able to bring aid into the most devastated areas & most vulnerable populations as quickly and efficiently. GEM's goal on the ground is to distribute aid in affected disaster zones in less than 48 hours after the disaster strikes, arriving in the immediate wake of loss with crucial, life-saving aid.
1309.activities: GEM prepositions emergency aid supplies such as non-perishable food items, water, hygiene products, and other life- saving goods such as temporary shelters, generators and medical supplies. GEM also partners with local grass-roots organizations to further impact the communities affected by these disasters. GEM’s average response time is 24-48 hours.
1309.direct_services: GEM implements a Family Necessity Kit program where those affected by disasters receive a box containing life- saving food, hygiene products, and other forms of aid that can support a family of 4 for up to a week. GEM also implements a Relief Card program where those affected by disasters receive a pre-loaded gift card containing $100- $500 to be able to replace essential goods & supplies.
1309.population: The funds will serve the general population in Florida, specifically ensuring the residents receive the aid & assistance they need before and after disasters strike. GEM expects to serve nearly 1 million individuals in Florida annually.
1309.outcome: GEM expects to ensure that all Florida residents feel prepared and safe before disasters. GEM also expects all Florida residents are not left behind in the aftermath of destructive disasters, such as major hurricanes. These outcomes will be measured by the number of individuals GEM is able to serve in Florida annually.

1495.description: Franklin County is seeking funding to conduct a comprehensive update of its local Comprehensive Plan, in accordance with Florida statutory requirements. This effort will ensure the Plan remains a legally compliant, forward-looking framework for guiding growth, land use, and infrastructure investment over the next decade. The project will include a full update of supporting data and analysis, integration of current demographic and environmental trends, and the drafting of revised plan language that reflects community priorities and regulatory standards. It will also involve the development of public presentations to support stakeholder engagement and transparency, as well as technical assistance throughout the state review and adoption process. This funding will enable the County to refresh all supporting data and analysis, revise policy language, facilitate public engagement, and guide
1495.activities: To fulfill the purpose of updating Franklin County’s Comprehensive Plan, the requested funds will support a comprehensive suite of planning activities and services. These include updating all supporting data and analysis to reflect current demographic, environmental, and land use conditions; drafting revised policy language that aligns with updated state guidance and local priorities; and developing public presentations and engagement strategies to ensure transparency and community input. The pr

In alignment with the updated requirements introduced by Senate Bill 180 (SB180), this project will ensure Franklin County’s Plan reflects current conditions, integrates resilience and mobility strategies, and supports coordinated development over a 10-year horizon. 2475.description: Boley Centers will renovate its behavioral health campus to improve safety, expand capacity, and create flexible space for medical treatment and recovery. The project supports comprehensive health care, substance use recovery, housing stabilization, and employment readiness. The project will also improve space to expand medical services offered through local medical health partners. These enhancements will decrease rates of homelessness, emergency room utilization, and criminal justice involvement, while advancing recovery, self-sufficiency, and community safety.
2475.purpose: Funds will renovate and rehabilitate Boley Centers’ main campus facilities to improve building safety, expand housing and service capacity, and create flexible space for medical and behavioral health service delivery. Renovations will support quality mental health and substance use treatment, recovery supports, and pathways to permanent housing and independence.
2475.activities: Funds will support renovations that allow Boley Centers to provide access to safe housing with on-site behavioral health treatment, substance use recovery services, and stabilization supports. Services include counseling, case management, skills training, and employment readiness programs, with flexible space for health care integration. These activities reduce crisis service use, homelessness, and justice system involvement while promoting recovery and independence.
2475.direct_services: Citizens will gain access to safe and rehabilitative housing paired with behavioral health treatment, substance use recovery supports, and case management services. Direct services include access to counseling, peer support, and vocational readiness programs. Renovated spaces will also allow delivery of integrated health services, ensuring individuals achieve improved health outcomes, reduced reli
2475.population: 750 individuals with serious & persistent mental illness.
2475.outcome: Improve Mental Health: Higher DLA-20 functioning scores; reduced suicide risk. Improve Physical Health: Reduced 911 calls; faster medical access; improved health outcomes. Reduced Substance Use: Greater access to substance abuse treatment & increased sobriety. Reduce Recidivism: Lower jail/crisis use through housing and treatment. Enhance Self-Sufficiency: Increased employment readiness, income, and insurance.

2476.organization: Chi Chi Rodriguez Youth Foundation, Inc.
2476.description: The Chi Chi Rodriguez Youth Foundation has been positively impacting the youth in Pinellas County for over 45 years. Our mission is to educate students in a public-private partnership and improve their academic performance, self-esteem, and character using the golf course as a living classroom. The project is the expansion and renovation of the Foundation's campus, providing more classrooms, enhanced safety and security, upgraded facilities & technology, and growing the living classroom relationship with the golf course.
2476.purpose: The expansion of the Chi Chi Academy campus will: expand classroom capacity, allowing our program to grow to 126 students from 96, while maintaining our student-to-teacher ratio that supports effective learning for at-risk students; enhance safety and security of the school, implementing controlled access points and secure entryways; and upgrade facilities by removing outdated portable classrooms with permanent structures.
2476.activities: The Foundation is working with an architect to design a safe and secure learning environment. The architect will work with the chosen contractors on implementing the build over the next two years through phased construction. The construction will be phased to focus on the least amount of disturbance possible throughout the school day.
2476.direct_services: The Chi Chi Academy public-private partnership school is a voluntary school for fifth through eighth grade students not achieving at their grade level, have low self-esteem or have difficulty adjusting to a larger academic environment. The Academy is a small school atmosphere, which thrives on individualized attention, counseling, real-life experiences in the Foundation's businesses (living classr
2476.population: The Chi Chi Academy serves students at risk for dropping out of high school in the future. Our students meet two or more of the following requirements: (1) face academic challenges, (2) require additional assistance with social skills, (3) have poor school attendance, (4) lack of a strong family support system, or (5) obtain some form of government assistance (over 70% considered economically disadvantaged). With the expansion, the Academy will serve 126 students each year. The Foundation serves
2476.outcome: The Foundation is determined to positively impact the graduation rate of our at risk youth population. The Academy gives our students the tools needed to enter and successfully graduate high school, with the ultimate goal of being a productive member of our community. Students success while at school are academically tracked with gains in the classroom and through state testing. Many of our students also struggle socially, and their successes are measured by behavior growth seen by their teachers and counselor.

1497.description: Franklin County is requesting funding to support a down payment for the replacement of the St. George Island Volunteer Fire Department’s (SGI VFD) aging aerial apparatus, which has been in service for over 25 years and has reached the end of its reliable operational life. The proposed replacement, a 2029 E-One 100' RM Aerial Platform, represents a modern, National Fire Protection Association-compliant ladder and tower truck designed to enhance emergency response capabilities, improve firefighter safety, and ensure continued operational readiness for the island’s volunteer fire service. This investment will directly support life safety, structural fire suppression, and rescue operations in a geographically isolated coastal community, where reliable equipment is critical to protecting residents, visitors, and property.
1497.purpose: The specific purpose of the requested funds is to provide a down payment for the replacement of Ladder 7, the St. George Island Volunteer Fire Department’s 25-year-old aerial apparatus, which has reached the end of its reliable service life. The proposed replacement—a 2029 E-One 100' RM Aerial Platform—will ensure continued operational readiness, enhance firefighter safety, and bring the department into compliance with current National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standards. This investmen
1497.activities: To meet the intended purpose of replacing the St. George Island Volunteer Fire Department’s aging aerial apparatus, the requested funds will support the following activities and services: • Procurement Coordination: Initiating the purchase process for the 2029 E-One 100' RM Aerial Platform, including securing the down payment and finalizing vendor agreements. • Compliance Assurance: Ensuring the new apparatus meets current National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standards for aerial equipmen
1497.direct_services: The 2029 E-One 100' RM Aerial Platform truck is essential to meeting both the current and future operational needs of the St. George Island Volunteer Fire Department. This modern aerial apparatus will significantly enhance the department’s ability to respond effectively to emergency situations, particularly in a community where 96% of single- family dwellings (1,539 out of 1,602) are two stories o

Franklin County has only two aerial apparatus units—one operated by SGI VFD and the other by Carrabelle VFD. If either unit is out of service, the county must rely on mutual aid from neighboring jurisdictions, which significantly increases response times and r
1497.outcome: The expected outcome of this project is the successful acquisition and deployment of a modern, NFPA-compliant aerial apparatus that replaces the aging Ladder 7 unit and restores full operational readiness to the St. George Island Volunteer Fire Department. This will improve emergency response times, enhance firefighter safety, and ensure reliable service for the island’s 1,100 residents and 20,000+ annual visitors. Success will be measured through completion of the purchase, compliance verification, operational testing, reduced reliance on mutual aid, and documented improvements in incident response capability.

1498.description: Franklin County seeks funding to install energy-efficient, storm-rated lighting at Sylvester Williams Park to improve safety, accessibility, and year-round usability. This lighting upgrade will complement a series of recent improvements made to the park, including the installation of new playground equipment, engineering for a paved parking area, removal of unsafe structures, gate and fencing repairs, updated safety signage, enhancements to the softball field, and extensive clearing of brush and trees. The proposed lighting will increase visibility for evening use, deter vandalism, and ensure the park remains a safe, welcoming space for residents and visitors—even during inclement weather. This investment supports the County’s broader commitment to resilient, inclusive, and well-maintained public spaces.
1498.purpose: Franklin County seeks funding to install energy-efficient, storm-rated lighting at Sylvester Williams Park to improve safety, accessibility, and year-round usability. 1498.activities: The installation of the Light Structure System at Sylvester Williams Park will integrate structural, electrical, and lighting components into a unified, high-performance solution. Engineered for long-term reliability in coastal and storm-prone environments, this system delivers precise, energy-efficient illumination while minimizing spill, glare, and light pollution. By directing light exactly where needed, it enhances safety and usability without disrupting surrounding natural areas. The system
1498.direct_services: The appropriation project will directly provide Franklin County residents with enhanced recreational services through the installation of energy-efficient, storm-rated lighting at Sylvester Williams Park. This improvement will extend safe access to the park during evening hours, support multi-generational use, and promote active play, wellness, and social interaction. Families, youth, seniors, and
1498.outcome: The expected benefit of this project is a safer, more accessible, and environmentally responsible Sylvester Williams Park through the installation of energy-efficient, storm-rated lighting. This upgrade will extend usable hours, improve visibility, deter vandalism, and support multi-generational recreation in a well-maintained public space. The outcome will be measured through successful installation and operational testing, verification of energy and resilience standards, increased evening park usage, reduced safety incidents, and resident feedback, demonstrating enhanced public safety, community engagement, and alignment with Franklin County’s infrastructure goals.

1265.description: Since 2023 DOE has been required to have a system to track all school district bond debt, FS 1009.90(13). Over $43 billion dollars have been raised by school districts using bond referendums. Prior to this system the state had little optics into the debt being incurred by districts until after the referendum was voted on and debt had been issued. The specific purpose is to have the legislature, OPB and DOE be able to know which districts are over leveraged before debt is issued as well as keep key language to ensure use of funds comply with the ballot language and purpose.
1265.purpose: The specific purpose is to have the legislature, OPB and DOE be able to know which districts are over leveraged before debt is issued as well as keep key language to ensure use of funds comply with the ballot language and purpose.
1265.activities: Tracking of all school board meetings and school board proposed as well as issued debt in near real time. keep a data base of all school board debt, date of issuance, date of termination and total debt upon districts statewide as well as individual school district debt.
1265.population: taxpayer protection by having state and DOE optics into district debt statewide. In past years the state has discovered school districts are over leveraged beyond state law limits, only after the bond had passed.
1265.outcome: Reporting and notification of proposed school issued debt before issued. Proper use of funds from bonds. Oversight on school districts exceeding debt limits.

1266.description: IMPOWER's Residential Substance Abuse Treatment Program in Winter Springs, FL provides treatment of opioid and other substance use addictions with co-occurring psychiatric diagnoses for youth 13-17. The facility is in need of capital improvements addressing safety and recreation spaces such as electrical upgrades, drainage repairs for current and future recreational spaces, windows/doors replacement.
1266.purpose: To provide a safe and therapeutic living environment for youth as they move through the treatment and recovery process. To provide a healing center for the mind, body and spirit.
1266.activities: Safer and better quality of life. More assessable kitchen and larger cafeteria. Expanded wellness center to have enough space for activities such as yoga, art therapy, physical exercise. Meeting space for training and treatment team. Office space located on campus close to clients.
1266.direct_services: Overall addictions treatment to include medical examinations, medical treatment and drug testing.
1266.population: Florida male and female adolescents between 13 and 18 yrs old who meet criteria for residential substance abuse treatment because they are addicted to one or more of the following: opioids, benzodiazepines, methamphetamine, (crack) cocaine, cannabis, alcohol, among others.
1266.outcome: Funding will assist IMPOWER in strengthening its holistic approach to helping youth with crippling chemical dependency issues build a foundation for long-term recovery/wellness. Outcomes will include sustained health and sobriety in youth who graduate the program and will be measured by % of youth who successfully complete the treatment program and % of youth who remain sober 1 year and 5 years post-discharge.

2477.description: Hurricanes Helene and Milton caused significant flooding and damage to South Pasadena's City Hall. The cost to repair the building is estimated to be above FEMA's 50% threshold. Built in 1975, the structure presents major ADA, code compliance, and resiliency issues in addition to the storm damage making repairs uneconomical. Funding is needed to build a resilient City Hall that can effectively serve the community and withstand future disasters.
2477.purpose: The specific purpose is to construct a resilient City Hall that will serve the community by providing safe and accessible government operations. Such services provided within City Hall include Commission meetings, Town Halls, elections, community outreach, and senior services. The facility houses multiple City departments including Administration and Finance which need a secure and effective facility to serve the public both in blue skies and in the event of a disaster.
2477.activities: Funding will be used for the construction of a resilient and accessible City Hall building. Construction will focus on an elevated, hardened structure with utilities designed to withstand disasters while providing adequate space for vital City services.
2477.direct_services: The construction of a new resilient City Hall will allow the City to resume vital services including the assembly of the City's elected governing body in a space that is adequately accessible to the public, the operations of key departments, customer service, public outreach, election services, and public hearings.
2477.population: The target population being served by the project is the community of South Pasadena and Pinellas County. The project will allow members of the public to effectively receive services which extends beyond the jurisdiction of South Pasadena. Prior to the damage sustained during Hurricanes Helene and Milton, City Hall had been a key location for numerous community organizations throughout the region and a new facility would allow for those outreach and engagement opportunities to resume and increas
2477.outcome: The expected benefit is the ability to resume and even increase services to the public, and that such services will be maintained following disasters. The project will be measured by the specific services that can be offered in a new facility, the decrease in downtime following disasters, and the increased efficiency of city services.

1267.outcome: Benefits: New construction of state-of-the-art research labs for teaching and research activities; increase classroom and lab availability; facilities to engage in productive industry partnerships. Outcomes: Increasing STEM enrollment and graduates for increasing the available talent pipeline and highly skilled workforce needed by Florida high-tech employers; increasing workforce in higher paying jobs; equipping graduates for innovation and start-ups; industry growth and expansion; higher median income levels.

1499.description: This project will design and construct a dedicated access road serving Dixie County High School by creating a dedicated entry and exit onto US-19. By separating the bus, parent, and staff traffic from this main corridor, the project will reduce the congestion and vehicle conflict points, improving safety for over 700 students and the surrounding community.

Currently, buses, parent vehicles, and staff share the same access points, creating daily congestion and safety hazards. By separating bus and parent traffic, this project will reduce vehicle conflict points, improve emergency response access, and ensure safer, more efficient transportation for more than 80

The project will also include safety enhancements such as traffic control signage, bus circulation design, and improved site visibility off and on US- 19. Activities will be managed by Dixie District Schools in coordination with design professionals to ensure compliance with FDOT, local, and Departm

Direct benefits include reduced traffic congestion on US-19 and local side streets, shorter travel and wait times for families, and a significant reduction in vehicle and pedestrian safety risks. The road will also serve as an alternate emergency access r

Secondary beneficiaries include parents, school transportation operators, and community members who travel through the US-19 corridor in Cross City. Collectively, the project will improve daily transportation safety and efficiency for more than 1,000 individuals and reduce congestion for hundreds of through-travelers on this critical local a

Enhanced student and pedestrian safety by eliminating shared access between buses and cars. Reduced transportation delays and improved on-time student arrival. Increased emergency access reliability for school facilities. Measurement Methods: Conduct before-and-after traffic volume and queue-length studies to measure congestion reduction. 1268.description: To protect limited state resources, UCF seeks to re-purpose an existing campus building, addressing critical deferred maintenance while adapting the space to meet the present and future needs of students. Renovations will centralize student support services to create a One Stop Student Success Hub including academic advising, financial, career services and registrar services. This renovation will extend the life of a 55-year old building, reducing future maintenance costs.
1268.purpose: One of UCF’s oldest buildings, Howard Phillips Hall is consistently ranked within the university’s Facilities Condition Assessment as a priority due to aging systems and the overall condition. Funding would support a full renovation of the interior of the building and building systems, in addition to comprehensively reconfiguring the building to optimize space utilization and support the strategic goals of the university. The renovation would allow the university to co-locate student success dep
1268.activities: After funds are expended for the remodeling and renovation, Howard Phillips Hall will house a new Student Success Center and will provide academic advising, financial aid, registrar and career services for UCF students. This renovation supports the State University System’s strategic priorities, including improving four-year graduation rates and enhancing student services to drive retention and career readiness.
1268.direct_services: The new Student Success Center in Howard Phillips Hall will provide academic advising, financial aid, registrar and career services for UCF students.
1268.population: Applicants, registered, and enrolled University of Central Florida students.
1268.outcome: Benefit: Student-centered and efficient design for the effective and efficient delivery of services to support student achievement, retention, and increasing 4-year graduation rates. This renovation supports the State University System’s strategic priorities, including improving four-year graduation rates and enhancing student services to drive retention and career readiness.

1500.description: As part of the District’s consolidation from four schools to three, this project increases Old Town Elementary’s capacity to offset classroom loss from Anderson Elementary’s closure. Enclosing existing covered play areas creates four new instructional spaces, maximizing savings by utilizing existing roof and foundations. A new covered walkway, designed per S.R.E.F. guidelines, enhances safety and connectivity for students.
1500.purpose: As part of the District’s consolidation from four schools to three, this project increases Old Town Elementary’s capacity to offset classroom loss from Anderson Elementary’s closure. Enclosing existing covered play areas creates four new instructional spaces, maximizing savings by utilizing existing roof and foundations. A new covered walkway, designed per S.R.E.F. guidelines, enhances safety and connectivity for students.
1500.activities: The District will engage the services of Design Professionals (Architect and Engineer) to design the new classrooms. After completion of construction documents, a licensed Contractor will be selected to construct the classrooms.
1500.direct_services: In addition to the 500 to 600 students that attend the school each day, the facility is a community hub. The spaces would be used for non-school related sporting events and outdoor community events. The classrooms may be used by local organizations for community events and meetings.
1500.population: 500-600 elementary school students and between 250-500 community members may use the classrooms for after school outdoor events.
