There is a demand for more hangars at the Airport and for a facility that can accommodate aviation related businesses. As a fiscally constrained county, economic growth is critically needed. The new station will be on County owned property in a centralized location.
1573.purpose: The goal is the construction of new primary Fire Station to be located at or near Perry-Foley Airport. The existing station is located in an old WW II aircraft hangar at the Airport. The new station will provide adequate equipment storage and living quarters for the County's full-time firefighters. The facility will enable the Airport to lease the hangar for aviation use, airport growth, and economic development opportunities. The primary Station serves all of Taylor County as well as provides m
1573.activities: The station will provide fire protection and emergency support services to the entire County. The facility will serve as the County's primary station. Though County owned, the fire station will be located just south of the central business district of the City of Perry. Numerous businesses and industry are located within 1/2 mile of the station. The station will be located less than 1/4 mile from US 19 a key roadway. Perry-Foley Airport is a general aviation airport that serves as a regional dis
1573.direct_services: Direct services will be the provision of fire protection and emergency response services to the entire County in a centralized location. The new station will enable the County to use the aircraft hangar Fire Rescue is currently located in for aviation and economic development purposes. The County does have other hangars located at Perry Foley airport however, they are all leased (and consistently
1573.population: The target population is the entire County (21,582). The Station will serve all areas of the County as well as provide mutual aid to the City of Perry. Mutual aid is also provided when so needed to the adjacent counties of Dixie, Lafayette, Madison and Jefferson.
1573.outcome: The benefit is an adequate facility to serve as the primary Fire Station for the County. The facility will have storage for vehicles, equipment, and apparatus as well as living quarters for full time firefighters. The new facility will enable the Airport to use the hangar the Station is currently located in for aviation purposes and economic development. The Airport has experienced considerable growth over the years and made numerous improvements with FDOT and FAA funding assistance.

3173.description: Taylor County (County) seeks funding for the construction of a hurricane rated fire station and public safety facility at Keaton Beach. The existing facility suffered considerable damages from Hurricanes Idalia and Helene as it is not a hurricane rated structure. Personnel currently evacuate the facility prior to coastal weather or potential flooding events leaving no fire protection or emergency support services in the Keaton Beach area. The new facility will not only be a hurricane rated structure, but it will also be constructed to code elevations to prevent flooding of the facility. The station will allow for the continuity of operations and disaster recovery efforts.
3173.purpose: Construction of a hurricane rated, elevated structure will provide for the continuity of operations of fire rescue and emergency support services at Keaton Beach as well as the communities of Dekle Beach, Dark Island, Spring Warrior, Cedar Island, and the southern end of the County. The Keaton Beach area is located 23.1 miles from the primary Fire Station in Perry as well as other emergency services. Steinhatchee offers limited fire and emergency services and is 19.3 miles away on roads which ar
3173.activities: The new building will serve as a public safety facility with the primary use being Fire Rescue services. In addition to fire protection and emergency services, the site will serve as a disaster recovery staging area.
3173.direct_services: Direct services will include but not be limited to fire protection, emergency support services, and disaster recovery. The new facility will provide services to the communities of Keaton Beach, Dekle Beach, Dark Island, Cedar Island, Spring Warrior, and Yates Creek as well as the south end of the County. In addition to direct services provided on a daily basis, the facility will ensure for rapid r
3173.population: The target population is Keaton Beach and the surrounding coastal communities as well as provide support for Steinhatchee. Approximately 5,000 citizens will be served year round with double that number being served in the very busy recreational boating, fishing, and scalloping seasons. The County also provides mutual aid to the nearby counties of Lafayette and Dixie.
3173.outcome: The project will provide a hurricane rated, resilient structure which will enable Fire Rescue to provide services in all types of conditions and weather events. Fire Rescue personnel, vehicles, and equipment will be able to shelter in place to provide fire and emergency services during tropical storms and immediately after major storms. Emergency response times will be substantially reduced with a resilient, hardened facility with adequate equipment and apparatus storage areas.

1569.agency: Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
1569.description: The project is the construction of a new animal shelter which will provide an adequate facility and critically needed resources to provide for the hundreds of animals Taylor County shelters annually. The County is the sole provider of animal control. The shelter is located in a structure constructed in 1957 which does not have adequate climate control, ventilation, and natural light. There have been on going drainage issues as the building was not originally constructed for use as an animal shelter. A study completed by the University of Florida has provided the County insight on shelter needs and facility requirements.
1569.purpose: The purpose is the construction of a new animal shelter that will provide a safe and healthy environment with adequate climate control, drainage, ventilation, and natural light. The shelter will have adequate sizes of kennels and separate dog and cat areas. The facility will have exercise areas as well as a meet and greet area which will aid in adoptions. A study conducted by the University of Florida Maddie's Shelter Medicine Program has outlined the County's sheltering needs and will be used t
1569.activities: The new facility will provide adequate facilities to care for both dogs and cats who are in the custody of Taylor County Animal Control. The shelter will be constructed to meet needs in a safe and healthy environment for both the animals and humans who provide for the care and services needed to place the animals in homes. Numbers have continued to rise of animals who are in the care of Animal Control and it is hoped the new facility will increase adoptions and assistance from transfer organizat
1569.direct_services: Taylor County is the sole provider of animal control in the County. Direct services will be a facility which will provide adequate animal services and care in the hopes of increasing adoptions and rescue services from other agencies better equipped to place animals in homes and better situations with a decrease in euthanasia. The new building will also provide for a facility that is adequately equ
1569.population: All citizens in Taylor County (21,582) will be served by the animal shelter as well as animal rescue groups and volunteers who assist the County with adoptions and/or fostering, medical care, and donations. Taylor County Board of County Commissioners is the sole provider of animal control and the humane investigation thereof in the County.
1569.outcome: The facility will provide adequate climate control, ventilation, natural light, and storage areas for supplies and food. There will be separate areas to efficiently accommodate dogs and cats with kennels with adequate space to accommodate various sizes of animals including mothers with their puppies or kittens. The new facility will provide sufficient areas for outdoor exercise. In addition, the new facility will have a meet and greet area which is essential for potential adopters to meet animals in need of homes in a friendly and safe environment.

1382.description: The Kosher Senior Meals Program provides culturally appropriate nutrition services to approximately 800 food-insecure seniors annually through Jewish Community Services of South Florida. Program funds offset higher kosher food costs, ensuring equal nutritional quality through home-delivered meals, congregate dining, and shelf-stable foods. This enables seniors to maintain their religious dietary requirements while aging with dignity at home, preventing unnecessary institutional care. No senior should compromise nutritional health due to religious observance.
1382.purpose: This funding will bridge the cost gap for kosher meal preparation, enabling the JCS Senior Meals Program to serve 800 seniors annually through home delivery and congregate sites with nutritionally equivalent meals that meet both dietary laws and nutritional standards. The purpose of the Senior Meals Program is to reduce food insecurity among seniors in Miami-Dade county by providing access to appropriate kosher meals that meet the Recommended Dietary Intake (DRI) guidelines.
1382.activities: The Program provides culturally appropriate nutrition services to approximately 800 food-insecure seniors annually through Jewish Community Services of South Florida. Program funds offset higher kosher food costs, ensuring equal nutritional quality through home-delivered meals, congregate dining, and shelf-stable foods. This enables seniors to maintain their religious dietary requirements while aging with dignity at home, preventing costlier institutional care. No senior should compromise nutrit
1382.direct_services: JCS provides kosher meals through home deliveries and at congregate meal sites, serving approximately 800 seniors annually. This ensures that older adults receive culturally appropriate, nutritious meals to support their well-being and dietary needs.
1382.population: The target population for these funds are homebound low-income seniors in Miami-Dade County who may be economically disadvantaged, in poor physical health, and physically disabled regardless of race, religion, ethnicity, or gender. We expect to serve approximately 800 seniors.
1382.outcome: Expected Benefits/Outcomes: Senior clients will maintain nutritionally balanced diets and enhance their quality of life while aging in place with independence, reducing use of institutional/residential care. Participants will experience decreased food insecurity. Measurement Methodology: Social workers and support staff will conduct annual assessments of nutritional risk and evaluate health and wellness of each senior client. Clients will complete feedback surveys to measure food security and satisfaction.

1668.description: As a community located on a barrier island, the Town of Golden Beach is consistently inundated with storm, tidal and ground water. Flood waters greatly impact the navigable state evacuation route for the barrier island communities. Within the community there are (3) islands. The southern most island is at the towns lowest elevation and currently relies on gravity to discharge storm water. We hope to enhance our storm water collection system already in place by installing a permanent forced storm water pump to the existing system, converting from gravity to forced. The forced system will reduce the possibility of illicit discharges from sewage systems that can greatly affect the surrounding pristine water bodies flowing into the Ocean, Intra-coastal, and Biscayne Bay.
1668.activities: Planning, Permitting, and installation of a new forced storm water pump station.
1668.direct_services: Relief from flood conditions that will allow ease of access for emergency vehicles and reduction of damage to private and town property. Reduction in possibility of illicit discarge from sewage systems that can flow into surrounding water bodies.
1668.population: Residents of Golden Beach and surrounding communities. There are (365) households in Golden Beach.
1668.outcome: A forced system will allow the swift discharge of flood water and avoid the possibility of illicit discharge from sewage systems. The system will allow for a reduction of damage to property by greatly reducing the time of standing water in our roads and right of ways.

1564.description: Funding is requested for the construction of a new inland well and treatment facility to replace an existing well located in the St. Marks Wildlife Refuge, which must be decommissioned due to lease expiration. This project will enhance system resiliency against flooding, improve operational redundancy, and ensure reliable water delivery. Funding also supports SCADA upgrades, emergency power replacement, and efficient metering through AMR technology.
1564.purpose: Funding will support the construction of a new inland well and treatment facility to replace an existing well located in the St. Marks Wildlife Refuge, which must be decommissioned due to lease expiration. The new well's capacity will be able to serve current customers and neighboring communities like Alligator Point and Sopchoppy, strengthening regional water security and resilience. Additional upgrades include advanced meters, emergency power, and SCADA monitoring.
1564.activities: Funding will support construction of a new inland well and treatment facility to replace a decommissioned well, enhancing resiliency and redundancy. It also includes SCADA upgrades for system efficiency, emergency generator replacement for backup power, and replacement of 1,200 aging water meters with AMR technology for accurate, remote monitoring.
1564.direct_services: Funding will deliver reliable potable water through a new inland well and treatment facility, reducing flood risk and improving redundancy. The new well's capacity will be able to serve current customers and neighboring communities like Alligator Point and Sopchoppy, strengthening regional water security and resilience. Other upgrades include advanced meters, emergency power, and SCADA monitoring.
1564.population: PAWS serves 1,164 utility customers, each using an average of 6,513 gallons of water per month.
1564.outcome: Once Well #8 is operational, it will replace nearly 50% of the system's current supply lost from Well #6, while SCADA and meter upgrades will improve monitoring accuracy, reduce water loss, and enhance billing efficiency. Methodologies to measure these outcomes include: comparing total gallons produced daily before and after Well #8 is operational, monitoring reductions in outages due to improved redundancy and emergency power, measuring improvements in response time and issue detection, and tracking billing discrepancies and leak detection rates after AMR meter installation.

1563.description: The City seeks funding to construct Well 7B, a fully permitted, shovel-ready project that will provide critical redundancy, improve emergency reliability, and ensure sustainable water service for Wakulla County's growing population. Site preparation is complete, and construction can begin immediately, delivering backup capacity, fire flow support, and long- term reliability for public safety and growth.
1563.purpose: The City seeks funding to construct Well 7B—a fully permitted, shovel-ready project with site prep complete. Hurricane Helene caused outages that halted water operations; Well 7B will provide redundancy for Well 7A, maintain service during severe weather, support fire flow and peak demand, and ensure long-term reliability for Wakulla County's growing population.
1563.activities: Activities include constructing Well 7B, installing pumps, motors, and controls, and connecting it to the water system. Services provided will ensure uninterrupted water supply, adequate fire flow, and operational flexibility during emergencies, maintenance, and future growth.
1563.direct_services: Funding will provide 12,500 citizens with reliable water service through construction of Well 7B, ensuring uninterrupted supply during emergencies, adequate fire flow, and operational flexibility. This enhances public safety, supports growth, and strengthens resiliency for Sopchoppy water system customers.
1563.population: The target population includes 12,500 citizens in Wakulla County who are served by the Sopchoppy water system.
1563.outcome: The project ensures consistent access to clean, safe water and adequate pressure for hygiene, sanitation, and fire flow—even during severe weather—reducing health risks and service disruptions. Outcomes will be measured by tracking water quality compliance reports, system uptime and pressure logs during emergencies, and reliability metrics during storms to confirm resilience and regulatory compliance.

1562.description: Hurricane Helene caused flooding, stormwater intrusion, and power outages in St. Marks, disrupting water service. To protect public health and ensure continuity, the City will upgrade infrastructure by replacing undersized lines and aging valves, adding hydrants, and extending mains along US 98. These improvements boost capacity, fire protection, and resilience against storms, safeguarding homes, businesses, and emergency response.
1562.purpose: Funding will replace undersized waterlines and aging valves, install new hydrants, and extend mains along US 98 to ensure reliable water service and fire protection—even during severe storms. These upgrades strengthen system capacity and resilience, safeguarding homes, businesses, and emergency response.
1562.activities: Funding will replace undersized 2-inch lines with 1,250 ft of 6-inch mains, upgrade isolation valves, and install new hydrants to improve hydraulic performance and fire flow. An additional 4,000 ft extension along US 98 will expand system capacity and resilience, ensuring reliable water delivery during severe weather.
1562.direct_services: The project will provide residents with reliable water service and improved fire protection by replacing undersized mains, faulty valves, and aging hydrants, and extending waterlines along US 98. These upgrades enhance system capacity, reduce service interruptions, and ensure safety during emergencies and severe weather.
1562.population: The St. Marks, FL public water system (PWS ID: FL1650630) serves approximately 643 people.
1562.outcome: Upgrades will reduce exposure to contaminants and improve fire protection by ensuring waterline integrity, reliable pressure, and safe drinking water. Outcomes will be measured by tracking compliance with drinking water standards, water quality reports, system uptime, boil-water advisories, fire flow tests, hydrant installations, and emergency response times before and after completion.

2137.description: Funding will be used to expand our certified community behavioral health center offering integrated comprehensive behavioral health and primary care including crisis intervention, screening and assessment, psychiatric evaluation, medication management, counseling, case management, care coordination and preventative and palliative primary care service for individuals with behavioral health conditions at risk of or who have 1 or more chronic diseases that are uninsured, under-insured and below 200% of the poverty level. Our goal is to improve access to care, improve health and behavioral health, prevent hospitalization and improve coordination of care.
2137.purpose: Our goal is to provide integrated health and behavioral health services to uninsured, under-insured and low income individuals with behavioral health conditions who are most at risk of chronic disease and early death due to a lack of healthcare. The goal is to improve access to care, improve health, behavioral health, and quality of life, reduce hospitalizations and improve coordination of care.
2137.activities: Services include expansion of crisis intervention, screening, assessment, psychiatric evaluation, medication management, counseling, case management, care coordination, support services and integrated primary care to include preventative care and palliative care.
2137.direct_services: Direct services that will be provided include crisis intervention, screening, assessment, psychiatric evaluation, medication management, counseling, case management, care coordination, support services, and integrated primary care to include preventative care and palliative care.
2137.population: Target population is individuals with behavioral health conditions that are also at risk for or have 1 or more chronic diseases. These individuals are uninusured, underinsured and are earning 200% or less of the poverty level.
2137.outcome: Access to care in 60 minutes for mobile crisis response, in 1 business day for urgent needs, 5 business days for post hospital discharges and 10 business days for routine care, 80% individuals served will improve their overall behavioral health symptoms, functioning and quality of life, 80% of individuals with 3 or more hospitalizations in past 6 months will reduce hospitalizations, 80% individuals served having one or more chronic diseases will will experience an improvement in health markers. Measured through DLA-20, PHQ-9, GAD-7, C-SSRS, ASAM, LOCUS administered at regular intervals, date of referral to date of first visit in in our EHR, hospitalization information measured in six month i

1977.description: This specialized outreach initiative is focused on reducing unsheltered homelessness by engaging, assessing, treating, and securing housing placement for persons who are homeless and hard to serve. The project will address immediate and long-term health and behavioral health needs, with the end goal of stabilization in housing.
1977.purpose: The goal is to reduce unsheltered homelessness using a specialized, multidisciplinary behavioral health outreach team, with a focus on homeless individuals with serious mental illness (SMI) and substance use disorders (SUD). Highly vulnerable individuals are engaged and connected to the comprehensive services they need to achieve stability, recovery, and ultimately, permanent housing.
1977.activities: The project will engage as many homeless individuals in Miami-Dade as possible, and deliver treatment and stabilization services along with housing and other supportive services.
1977.direct_services: The project will engage, assess, treat (medically and mentally) and secure supportive housing placement for persons who are homeless and mentally ill or have substance use disorders or co-occurring disorders living on the streets of Miami-Dade County.
1977.population: The project will serve 25-40 individuals with poor physical/mental health, drug users, homeless, physically disabled, jobless persons, economiclly disadvanteged persons, and chronically homeless individuals.
1977.outcome: Improve physical health indicators for participants by increasing access to healthcare services and reducing preventable health issues within 12 months of program enrollment. -Collect baseline data on participants physical health status, including chronic conditions, preventive care, and recent hospital or emergency department use. -Track engagement in medical appointments, screenings, vaccinations, and treatment adherence through case management records. -Use standardized clinical assessments (e.g., for depression, GAD-7 for anxiety, substance use screenings) and treatment adherence logs to track improvements. Reduce risks to the general public from criminal activity and unsafe behaviors am

1685.description: The Lord's Place currently houses 37 families, with a total of 70 children, at its Family Campus. These children and families would have otherwise continued to be homeless. We have an opportunity to create an environment that will foster youth development activities and a sense of normalcy for these children. A new youth center would allow us space to have tutoring, a community kitchen where we could teach families how to cook, and have recreational space for the children to learn and grow.
1685.purpose: The Lord's Place is seeking funding to build a small youth center on its family campus that houses 37 families, including 70 school aged youth. The facility would provide a safe place for children to get additional academic supports, engage in healthy play, and be provided with healthy snacks/meals during out of school time.
1685.activities: A new youth center would allow us space to have tutoring, life skills classes, a community kitchen where families can learn how to cook, and have recreational space for the children to learn and grow. Other youth development and prosocial activities will take place at the youth center throughout the week as well.
1685.direct_services: Minimally 70 children will receive education and youth development services (not covered by this request). This will divert children from at-risk behaviors and provide a sense of normalcy for children that would have otherwise been homeless.
1685.population: School aged children who would otherwise be homeless, who are economically disadvantaged and at-risk.
1685.outcome: Children residing at The Lord's Place Family Campus will have the opportunity to attend the youth center during out of school time, receive tutoring services and academic supports, life skills sessions, healthy eating demonstrations, and prosocial activities. This will keep youth out of trouble and safe while their parents work toward economic self- sufficiency. Each child's grades and academic progress will be tracked, as well as their attendance to the youth center each day/week.

2140.description: This program equips high school students and adults with technical training, mentorship, and direct pathways to aviation industry careers. By aligning education with workforce demand, it connects individuals to meaningful employment while addressing the sector’s shortage of skilled technicians. The program provides an alternative to the traditional four-year college path, expanding access to career opportunities for young adults, especially those from underserved or low- income communities. It also supports adults seeking to transition into a high-demand field that offers strong wages, career stability, and long-term growth.
2140.purpose: To prepare high school students and adults for careers in the aviation industry delivering accelerated, industry-aligned training, mentorship, and certifications providing direct pathways into high-demand fields such as Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO) and Fixed Base Operations (FBO). By connecting participants with hands-on experience and career opportunities, the program addresses Florida’s aviation workforce needs while fostering long-term economic growth and job stability.
2140.activities: The program will deliver accelerated technical training courses, industry-recognized certifications, and micro- credentials in aviation specialties such as MRO and FBO. Participants will receive hands-on instruction, career mentorship, and direct connections to employers through internships and job placement services. Additional services include academic support, soft skills development, and wraparound guidance to ensure long-term success in aviation careers.
2140.direct_services: Citizens will receive free or low-cost technical career training, hands-on instruction, and industry-recognized certifications in aviation fields. The program also provides mentorship, internships, job placement support, and wraparound guidance, creating direct pathways to stable, high-paying careers in the aviation industry.
2140.population: The program targets high school students, young adults, and career-transitioning adults, with a focus on individuals who may lack access to higher education or specialized training. In its first year, the program is expected to serve approximately 50–200 participants, with capacity to expand annually as demand and resources grow.
2140.outcome: Expansion of Florida’s skilled aviation workforce by creating stable, high-paying career pathways for residents. Expected outcomes include increased completion of industry-recognized certifications, strong job placement rates, and measurable contributions to the aviation sector and regional economy. Outcomes will be measured through pre- and post-program surveys on participant confidence and resilience, tracking of certifications and micro-credentials earned, internship and employment placement data, employer feedback, and long-term follow-up on career progression.

2141.description: A collaborative initiative between Nova Southeastern University and the Fort Lauderdale Police Department aimed at addressing unsolved homicide cases through student-supported investigative teams. The program leverages the skills and energy of criminal justice students to enhance investigative capacity, apply modern forensic techniques, improve case organization, and incorporate digital investigation strategies under expert supervision. Beyond its immediate impact on Fort Lauderdale’s 353 open homicide cases, the program serves as a model for statewide replication, strengthening Florida’s public safety system.
2141.purpose: The funds requested will support the Fort Lauderdale Cold Case Reduction Program by enhancing investigative capacity for unsolved homicide cases. Specifically, the funding will enable the supervision of student research teams, the application of modern forensic and digital investigation techniques, and the organization and preservation of case files, all aimed at generating leads, reopening cases, and increasing the likelihood of achieving justice for victims’ families.
2141.activities: The program will engage supervised student research teams to review and analyze cold case files, apply modern forensic and digital investigation techniques, organize and digitize case documentation, and assist in generating investigative leads. These activities will support the Fort Lauderdale Police Department in reopening unsolved homicide cases and improving overall case management and investigative efficiency.
2141.direct_services: The appropriation project will provide citizens with enhanced public safety and justice by supporting the investigation of unsolved homicide cases. Families of victims gain renewed hope for case resolution, while the broader community benefits from increased law enforcement capacity, more efficient case management, and the potential for arrests and closure in long-standing cases.
2141.population: The target population includes families of victims of unsolved homicides in Fort Lauderdale, the general community that benefits from enhanced public safety, and criminal justice students gaining hands-on experience. The program directly impacts the families connected to the city’s 353 open homicide cases, while indirectly serving the tens of thousands of residents and visitors who rely on a safer community environment.
2141.outcome: The Cold Case Reduction Program is expected to increase the likelihood of solving unsolved homicide cases, provide closure and justice for victims’ families, enhance public safety, and strengthen investigative capacity within the Fort Lauderdale Police Department. Additionally, it will provide students with practical experience in law enforcement and forensic science, preparing them for careers in these fields. The outcomes can be measured by tracking the number of cold cases reviewed, leads generated, cases reopened, and arrests made as a result of student-supported investigations. Student engagement and training outcomes can be assessed through participation records, project evaluations, a

1362.description: Description: According to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, the State of Florida generates approximately 1.1 million tons of residential glass, of which only 18% is reported to be recycled annually. This project would establish regional waste glass collection and processing facilities. Objective: Develop three regional waste glass processing facilities and create end markets for processed glass aggregate, with a strong focus on local economic development and sustainable market growth. This initiative will position Florida as a leader in sustainable glass recycling while driving economic growth and strengthening local markets for recycled materials.
1362.purpose: This initiative would develop three regional waste glass processing facilities in Florida and create end markets for processed glass aggregate.
1362.activities: Collection of waste glass from curbside recycling programs and drop-off centers, and Goodwill donation off facilities and process waste glass to glass aggregate for use in concrete applications, road base applications as well as in septic drain field applications.
1362.direct_services: This project will provide direct environmental and economic benefits to Florida citizens by expanding access to convenient glass recycling services, reducing landfill disposal costs, and supporting local job creation. Residents will gain new opportunities to recycle household glass, while communities benefit from cleaner environments, improved waste management infrastructure, and locally produced
1362.population: Florida Panhandle, Southeast and Southwest Florida residents. The total population as of the 2020 Census, was 1.5 million, 9.4 million and 2.2 million respectively. Using this figure, the regional populations as percentages of the state's total are: Florida Panhandle: Approximately 6.96%, Southeast Florida: Approximately 44.04%, and Southwest Florida: Approximately 6.99%.
1362.outcome: The project will be able to process 10,000 tons of waste glass. This equates to avoided disposal cost savings of $420,000 per year. Total tons of materials diverted from landfill as well as the volume of processed glass aggregate created as a result of the project.

2065.description: Funding would be for construction, repair, and improvements to the pump station and three critical water control structures on Southern Blvd to maintain water levels, prevent flooding, protect agriculture, and safeguard local infrastructure. These improvements strengthen long-term water-management reliability, support agricultural and equestrian operations, and reduce emergency response costs. The project also provides regional benefit by improving flood-control performance on the Southern Blvd corridor and supporting shared objectives with the SFWMD. The project is shovel-ready, regionally significant, and aligns with SFWMD priorities, providing high value and low implementation risk.
2065.purpose: Retrofit/modernize the pump station & three critical water control structures on Southern Blvd to maintain water levels, prevent flooding, protect agriculture, & safeguard local infrastructure. These improvements strengthen long-term water- management reliability, support agricultural & equestrian operations, and reduce emergency response costs. The project also provides regional benefit by improving flood-control performance on the Southern Blvd corridor & supporting shared objectives w/ SFWMD.
2065.activities: The project provides regional benefit by improving flood-control performance on the Southern Blvd corridor and supporting shared objectives with the SFWMD. This project is required to avert and mitigate flooding and potential storm damage and disaster--the control structures and single pump that the stormwater system relies upon are over 50 years old with significant unaddressed deferred maintenance. The project is shovel-ready, regionally significant, and aligns with SFWMD priorities, providing
2065.direct_services: maintain water levels, prevent flooding, protect agriculture and safeguard local infrastructure.
2065.population: This will serve the general population of Loxahatchee Groves and will feed safe water into the regional water system.
2065.outcome: Will strengthen regional flood protection, improve stormwater flow, reduce road washouts on rural areas without adjacent roads, protect the agricultural industry livestock and enhance operational stability for this industry. Will rehabilitate neglected infrastructure related to drainage and stormwater flooding.

2067.description: In response to the recent premature failure of a 36" stormwater pipe between two residential properties, which resulted in $300,000 replacement project and was likely caused by faulty installation, the Village proposes to video the existing 6,850' drainage pipe system connected to this incident, analyze each pipe for faults, and use FDOT-specified methodology to repair issues in place with minimal impact to residents. If faulty pipe cannot be repair in place, they will be removed and replaced.
2067.purpose: Prevent both short- and long-term damage to health and property caused by collapsed, faulty drainage pipes while also increasing the efficiency of the drainage system of residential neighborhoods.
2067.activities: Key drainage pipes will be investigated internally. Once they are audited, repairs or replacements will commence.
2067.direct_services: Residents receive direct protection from standing water by having damaged drainage pipes repaired and faulty ones replaced or fixed, using minimally disruptive methods. 3101.description: The current Police Department facility in Lake Placid is approaching 50 years old and lacks the necessary storm-rating to withstand severe weather conditions. This situation poses a safety risk for personnel and compromises emergency response capabilities. To address this pressing need, the Town has allocated $1.6 million locally towards the renovation and modernization of the facility. We are seeking an additional $800,000 to complete the construction.
3101.purpose: A new Police Station will provide for the safety of our staff and officers, particularly in the event of a hurricane. It will also improve the functionality of our Police Department in increased response since the current building is not safe to occupy during a hurricane event.
3101.activities: The construction of the new police department will provide for the health and safety of the staff and officers during severe weather events as well as provide adequate security for all property and evidence at the department allowing the agency to seek accreditation.
3101.direct_services: Public health and safety. Our Town has limited resources dedicated to public safety and our officers respond to many medical emergencies until EMS can arrive from other areas of the county.
3101.population: The citizens of the Town of Lake Placid as well as the surrounding community as our officers respond as backup for the local sheriff's office until other deputies can arrive from other areas of the county.
3101.outcome: A new, storm rated, hardened building will provide a safe location for our staff and officers.

2965.description: Funding needed to complete the expansion of this critical asset that is essential for providing safe, reliable drinking water to residents and businesses in this Rural Area of Opportunity. The Water Treatment Plant Expansion will increase capacity from 932,000 gallons per day (GPD) to 1,432,000 GPD. The existing 500,000 GPD ultrafiltration train has no backup, creating a reliability risk. The project will add a second 500,000 GPD ultrafiltration train to provide redundancy, ensure Class I reliability and protect public health. Improvements to include proper removal and disposal of residuals (sludge), water conservation measures and enhanced resiliency against pollution of water resources such as the Caloosahatchee River Estuary, Lake Okeechobee Basin (BMAP areas), and groundwater wells.
2965.purpose: Goal is to provide quality drinking water, improve life, health and safety. Funds need to expand Water Treatment Plant from 932,000 GPD to 1,432,000 GPD by adding a second 500,000 GPD ultrafiltration train. 2965.population: Target population is citizenry, visitors and residents of City of Moore Haven, Glades County, which is designated as a Rural Area of Opportunity, financially disadvantaged municipality. Target population is greater than 12,000.
2965.outcome: Benefits include safe, reliable drinking water, reduced service interruptions, and protection of natural resources. Protection of residents, commercial users, visitors, the environment from harm with improved water quality, increased capacity and flows; keeping pollution from water resources with proper treatment and disposal methods of residuals in this Rural Area of Opportunity located in the Caloosahatchee & Lake Okeechobee BMAP areas. Meeting Clean Water Act and permitting agencies rules/regulations is achieved with increasing capacity and flows from 932,000 GPD to 1,432,000 GPD.

Every year, over 350,000 cardiac arrests happen outside of a hospital. Sadly, only 10% survive. CPR especially if performed immediately and the use of an AED, can double or triple chances of survival! The Defibrillate Manatee Foundation is a non-profit organization located in Manatee County, Florida, but providing services to the entire state of Florida dedicated to saving lives from sudden cardiac arrest by distributing CPR Training Kits and Automated External Defibrillators (AEDs) to non-profit organizations and schools as well as providing CPR

These training resources will be provided to schools at no cost.

By giving someone CPR you can double or even triple their chances of survival.

2554.description: Funds are needed to support the completion of the multiyear project to relocate FPUA's wastewater treatment plant off of the Indian River Lagoon. Estimated to cost $195 million including construction of new plant (2026 end), redirection of the wastewater flow (2028 end), and decommissioning of the existing plant (2028 end). The project has already been approved by the City of Fort Pierce and FPUA has already secured a $100 million bond toward the total cost, plus $74M in grant requests approved to date.
2554.purpose: Funds are needed to support the completion of the multiyear project to relocate FPUA's wastewater treatment plant off of the Indian River Lagoon. While construction of the new treatment plant will be complete in January 2026, much work remains to re-route the flow of wastewater to the new plant. Estimated to cost $195 million including construction of new plant (2026 end), redirection of the wastewater flow (2028 end), and decommissioning of the existing plant (2028 end). The project has already
2554.activities: The conveyance system will be re-routed through the completion of 17 smaller projects throughout the wastewater service territory. Projects include installation of new pipes, construction of booster stations to pressurize flow to the new plant, and retrofits of pre-existing Lift Stations to redirect flow, among other projects. This funding will be used to support the completion of one or more of those sub-projects, working toward full completion of the relocation effort.
2554.direct_services: Wastewater treatment and disposal are critical for protecting public health. The current wastewater treatment plant is over 50 years old and sits on the vulnerable Indian River Lagoon. The new wastewater plant will be a state-of-the-art plant that is off of the lagoon, ensuring a healthy public as well as a healthy environment.
2554.population: All of FPUA wastewater customers will be served by this project, estimated at over 60,000 individuals. Although St. Lucie County is one of the fastest growing counties in State, Fort Pierce poverty levels are more than twice the poverty level of the state of Florida (26% in Fort Pierce compared to 12.3% Florida). These funds will be serving a largely low- income community, at a time when that community is also quickly adapting to rapid growth.
2554.outcome: This project will ensure that 5.75 million gallons per day of sewage is no longer sent through the vulnerable Indian River Lagoon for treatment. Funds will supplement the $100M of already-spent local funds to help ensure that this major project is seen through to completion in a timely and cost effective manner. Measurements will include: # of MGD sewage directed to the new treatment plant, # of storm events that we are protected from when the new plant is live, # of contracted workers benefiting from project activities, and # of gallons of reuse water directed to the neighboring power plant

3491.description: The purpose of the project is to establish a Central Receiving Facility (CRF) for St. Lucie, Okeechobee, Indian River, and Martin counties. The CRF is projected to provide behavioral health 72,000 services to more than 10,000 residents of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee.
3491.purpose: The CRF will provide 24/7 access for all individuals to crisis assessment, brief interventions, referral services, transitional care, and coordinated connection to outpatient service providers; improving behavioral health outcomes for residents of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee County and reducing emergency room visits and law enforcement contact.
3491.activities: The CRF will provide initial assessments, triage, case management, care coordination and related recovery services including detoxification and crisis stabilization. The CRF is project to provide 72,500 services annually.
3491.direct_services: Direct services to be provided to citizens will include Baker Act screening by qualified professional staff; referral and transportation to appropriate hospital beds when admission is needed for stabilization; triage and linkage to community behavioral health services as needed.
3491.population: This project will serve the citizens of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee counties that are experiencing a behavioral health crisis and in need of a Baker Act screening to determine level of risk of harm to self or others.
3491.outcome: Anticipated outcomes include increased access to emergency mental health services, measured by decreased wait times for evaluation and admission; increased community presence of law enforcement through reduced drop-off times when transporting individuals to the CRF for Baker Act screening; decrease in arrest, incarceration, and crime by the individuals served by this program as measured by longitudinal data for persons engaged in services; and improved functioning for individuals with diagnosed substance use disorder that engage in services as measured by the Functional Assessment Scale.

3492.organization: New Horizons of the Treasure Coast
3492.description: The purpose of the project is to secure non-recurring funding for capital improvements for Crisis Stabilization and behavioral health outpatient facilities.
3492.purpose: New Horizons of the Treasure Coast seeks nonrecurring state funding to address critical facility improvements necessary to maintain operations and meet insurance underwriting requirements. The requested funds will enable essential upgrades to our behavioral health facilities, ensuring we can continue providing appropriate mental health services to uninsured individuals across our service area. These improvements will directly benefit residents of the Treasure Coast.
3492.activities: Capital Improvements will allow New Horizons to continue providing behavioral health crisis and outpatient services to uninsured and under-insured residents of St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, and Okeechobee counties. Facility upgrades enable us to provide appropriate care to our clients. The funds are primarily used for our inpatient clients -- Adult Crisis, Detox, Short Term Residential and Transitional Group Home. Additionally, our outpatient 709 facility will be improved.
3492.direct_services: Uninsured and under-insured citizens will receive crisis stabilization, inpatient detox, outpatient therapy, case management, and psychosocial rehabilitation services.
3492.population: New Horizons is project to provide behavioral health services to 14,000 residents (adults and children) diagnosed with a serious mental illness or at-risk of a mental health crisis.
3492.outcome: Continual access to behavioral health crisis and outpatient services.

This project is for an approximate 0.48-mile stretch of SW 82 Ave, within Village Right of Way, between SW 160 St and SW 152 St. Improvements include: removal of existing striping and installation of new roadway & bike lane signage along the corridor; reducing the existing travel lanes to 10-ft wide; and constructing slight widening of the asphalt pavement to accommodate 4-ft-wide bike lanes and 1-ft buffer on each side of the road, as per FDOT Standard Index 711-002.
1377.purpose: The specific goal is to make the roadway safer for pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorists.
1377.activities: Activities that improve safety include: removal of existing striping and installation of new roadway & bike lane signage along the corridor; reducing the existing travel lanes to 10-ft wide; and constructing slight widening of the asphalt pavement to accommodate 4-ft-wide bike lanes and 1-ft buffer on each side of the road, as per FDOT Standard Index 711-002.
1377.direct_services: Motorists, pedestrians, and bicyclists who travel the area will benefit from safer road conditions and improved traffic flow.
1377.population: The target population includes residents of North and South Miami-Dade County who use the road regularly.
1377.outcome: The expected outcome of this project is to improve transportation conditions for all pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorists traveling through SW 82 Avenue by providing safer and more favorable transportation conditions. This outcome will be measured by documenting the decrease of accidents on SW 82 Avenue from SW 160 Street to SW 152 Street, quantifying the amount of people utilizing roadways, paths/sidewalks, and bike lanes, and recording the number of traffic complaints received by Village Hall.

The study will analyze population demand, site location, land acquisition needs, treatment technology, and costs for an 850,000 GPD plant. This effort will address failing septic systems that currently release harmful nutrients into the watershed, prevent 12.6 tons of nitrogen and 3 tons of phosphorus annually from entering state waters, and prepare for new large developments, such as Lakefront Estates.

The study will also evaluate environmental impacts, regulatory requirements, and long-term operational needs for a centralized wastewater system.
2558.direct_services: The feasibility study will directly benefit citizens by preparing the appropriate methods needed for the removal of old, failing septic systems in close proximity to Lake Okeechobee, Kissimmee River and the rim canal, reducing the release of nutrients and pathogens into canals, surface and groundwater. The study will enable future infrastructure that improves public health, protects private wells,

The project benefits the State and a broader regional
2558.outcome: The expected outcomes include a completed feasibility study that provides engineering, environmental, and financial data necessary to advance a new wastewater treatment plant for the northeast service area. Benefits will be realized through readiness for septic-to-sewer conversions, improved wastewater management planning, and anticipated reductions in nutrient loading to Lake Okeechobee and Kissimmee River The outcomes will be measured by the completion and approval of the study, the identification of viable sites and treatment alternatives, modeled pollutant load reductions, and the production of cost estimates and implementation strategies that can be used to move forward with design, lan

2559.description: Glades County and the City of Moore Haven through the City County Public Works Authority (CCPWA) continues to reduce TMDLs, protect State water resources, improve life, remove blight, health, safety, property & the environment. Funds are needed to design and construct wastewater infrastructure allowing for the removal of 82 old, failing septic systems in Washington Park, a low-income neighborhood, near the mouth of the Caloosahatchee River. The project is a gravity sewer system with laterals, lift stations, and force mains. roadway infrastructure upgrades, that improves water quality in the Lake Okeechobee and Caloosahatchee River BMAP areas, reduces pollutant loadings; meeting all permitting agency regulations.
2559.purpose: The goal is to improve life, health, property and the environment through improved wastewater infrastructure. Project is to design and install new wastewater infrastructure in the Washington Park community, a low income area that provides for modern sanitary sewer collection system allowing for the remaining 82 failing septic systems to be connected to the regional wastewater treatment facility, reducing pollutants and total maximum daily loads (TMDLs) entering the mouth of Caloosahatchee River
2559.activities: Glades County and the City of Moore Haven through the City County Public Works Authority (CCPWA) will seek contractual services through procurements policies and procedures for engineering, design, permitting, bidding, project management/administration, and engineering during construction, on-site construction observation and construction for the installation of gravity sewer mains, laterals, lift station, and force main, roadway upgrades and necessary infrastructure to allow for connection to t
2559.direct_services: Direct services to citizens is improved life, eliminating blight, health and safety with the appropriate wastewater infrastructure in place that includes roadway infrastructure upgrades. Project allows for the removal of 82 old, deteriorating/failing septic systems that now pollute and leach into State protected waters, Caloosahatchee River Basin and Estuary that flows west into Lee County and Lak
2559.population: The project serves the State of Florida by reducing pollutants from entering critical state protected waters of the Caloosahatchee River and Lake Okeechobee BMAP areas, thereby supporting environmental restoration and economic development and tourism. Glades County is designated as a Rural Area of Opportunity.
2559.outcome: The expected benefits are improved wastewater management, protection of surface, ground and drinking water, quality by reducing nitrogen and phosphorus discharges. Phase 2 will remove 1,197 pounds of nitrogen and 479 pounds of phosphorus annually from entering water tables and critical state waters. Success will be measured by certification of project completion, pollutant load reduction modeling, water quality testing, and the documented removal of 82 septic systems within 90 days after the infrastructure is in place. Also removes blight and upgrades roadway infrastructure.

1194.description: Our program is designed to create and formulate a long term work experience training program for individuals with autism and other developmental and intellectual disabilities in an educational setting. Our objective is to enhance transition planning and career development for these individuals. Some of the innovative features of our program include: *Customized employment opportunities, work experience, and transition planning for each student, driven by the student's interests, support needs, strengths, and contributions rather than by generic job descriptions and available openings. Customized implies flexibility and creativity enabling support staff to modify parameters and desired outcomes as the student's interests and skills evolve. *Enterpreneurial options or self-employment as post school outcomes or career experience options for students, in addition to traditional wage employme

The ratings are: progressing, needs work, satisfactory, good, exceptional.

COI, Inc. is an innovative approach to interrupt that pattern by collaborating with FDC to rebuild families with wellness, literacy, civic and STEM learning experiences that support both children and their incarcerated parent's improvements as a family unit. The program started in South Florida and has expanded to most of the metropolitan areas, serving over 2,800 families with over 7,000 children to date. COI, Inc. worked with a warden to design special child-focused visitation focused on reassuring the children about their parent’s safety, improving parenting and addressing behavioral issues. COI’s Family Strengthening, in collaboration with FDC, is proven to interrupt this pattern with supervised visitation/support services. 1930.description: This project will expand the existing wastewater treatment plant's capacity by 2,400,000 gallons per day, enhancing its ability to manage and treat wastewater effectively. The expansion will support the city's growing community needs, improve environmental sustainability, and ensure the facility can continue to meet regulatory standards while safeguarding public health and water quality.
1930.purpose: The requested funds are expeditiously needed to better serve the public. This project will expand the existing wastewater treatment plant's capacity by 2,400,000 gallons per day, enhancing its ability to manage and treat wastewater effectively. The expansion will support growing community needs, improve environmental sustainability, and ensure the facility can continue to meet regulatory standards while safeguarding public health and water quality.
1930.activities: The grant funds will be used to expand wastewater treatment services to residential, commercial, and industrial properties, including developers and builders currently in various stages of development. The expansion will ensure that these properties have access to a reliable centralized wastewater treatment system supporting sustainable growth and meeting environmental and regulatory standards.
1930.direct_services: Funding will support expanding wastewater treatment services for newly constructed residential, commercial, and industrial developments. This will provide reliable wastewater collection and treatment, ensuring public health, environmental protection, and sustainable growth. The expansion will also promote economic development and enhance local infrastructure.

The level of benefit will be measured by the number of properties successfully connected to the centralized wastewater treatment system, eliminating the need for package treatment plants, septic tanks, or other less effective wastewater treatment methods. This will demonstrate the project's success in improving wastewater management and environmental sustainability.

The SMP will identify and prioritize capital improvement projects to address stormwater needs across the community as well as develop a long-term Operations & Maintenance Plan to ensure sustainability. This project will evaluate the upstream and downstream stormwater needs of the City that will seek to identify modelled and known areas prone to flooding throughout the City including downtown, SR50 and Sampey Road subsequent drainage basins.
1931.purpose: Development of a city-wide storm water master plan to help the City of Groveland effectively manage storm water runoff, to protect water quality and the environment.
1931.activities: The storm water master plan document will include evaluation of culverts, swales and ditches, retention ponds, wet storage, park space, grass swales, land acquisition, and other alternatives to slow peak runoff. The planning document will ultimately recommend design and construction projects.

The planning document will ultimately recommend design and construction projects.

The Education Center will expand public access to green spaces while promoting water stewardship through interactive, hands-on learning. Exhibits will feature engaging content dedicated to highlighting the history of the site and its importance to water quality, wildlife, and public health.

Exhibits will utilize innovative teaching techniques, such as integrating hands-on, outdoor learning, to improve the quality of education for all visitors to the site.

This facility will replace an unsafe, inadequate existing structure with a resilient, hardened building designed to withstand severe weather events. Once completed, the center to serve as a resilient hub for evacuation center during storm events, recreational and social services center, food pantry, a year-round hub for recreation, fitness, established food distribution events, and social services. The center will directly improve safety, health, resilience, and quality of life for residents, 1st responders of this financially disadvantaged municipality.

2885.description: The South Howard Flood Relief project includes the design and construction of a major stormwater drainage system to relieve flooding along S. Howard Avenue, W. Swann Avenue, and adjacent neighborhoods. It includes the addition of more than 8,000 linear feet of box culvert and pipes as well as new drainage inlets and a new stormwater outfall to Hillsborough Bay to relieve flood conditions; upgraded water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure, undergrounding of overhead powerlines (in coordination with TECO) and improved water quality discharges to Hillsborough Bay through innovative green infrastructure technologies.
2885.purpose: Project will relieve street flooding up to the 5-year/8-hour (5.2-inch) storm event, which addresses flooding from most wet season events. It is generally expected that in greater events, some street flooding will occur and the goal shifts to maintaining at least one lane of traffic in each direction passable on major roadways. In extreme events – up to 100- year storm conditions – the goal becomes minimizing structural damage.
2885.activities: Construction of a major stormwater drainage system to relieve flooding along S. Howard Avenue.
2885.population: Residents, workers and visitors to the South Howard corridor and surrounding neighborhoods.
2885.outcome: Traffic flow during rain events with a minimum of one travel lane open even during unusually high rain events.

The Hub will support multiple programs, including Adopt-a-Classroom, which provides essential supplies to students and teachers; the Career Closet, offering professional clothing and career readiness support to underserved young adults and homeless individuals; and Respect the Ride, which delivers motorcycle safety and road-sharing education. Respect the Ride workshops will provide motorcycle safety education. The program will also support Adopt-A-Classroom efforts to supply schools with needed materials and strengthen community outreach.

The project will also deliver Respect the Ride motorcycle safety education and Adopt-a-Class
1313.population: The project will serve underserved youth, young adults, low-income families, and homeless individuals in the community. Services will also reach residents seeking employment support and those participating in motorcycle safety education. The project is expected to serve more 1,000's of individuals annually through clothing assistance, career readiness services, classroom support, and safety workshops.
1313.outcome: The project is expected to increase economic self-sufficiency, improve access to essential resources, and enhance community safety. Services support parents who do not have custody of their children, are unemployed or underemployed and are having difficulty meeting their child support obligations.
