Supporting documentation will include agendas or travel materials, competition awards, and college or scholarship applications. These outcomes will be verified through paperwork submitted by high school administration, statistical accountability reports, and community service logs.

3036.description: JCS Delivers provides tailored grocery delivery to current Home-Delivered Meals clients, filling a critical gap for items not covered by existing benefits. The program offers deliveries every two weeks valued at up to $250 each month directly to clients' doors, enabling homebound seniors to age in place. The program is unique in that is provides food twice a month, and social worker care for homebound seniors to avoid government-funded residential placements. These seniors live with dire economic conditions and rely on this source of food in order to maintain their health and age with dignity. Requested funds will support staff hours and grocery costs to meet increasing client needs.
3036.purpose: JCS Delivers provides tailored grocery delivery to current Home-Delivered Meals clients, filling a critical gap for items not covered by existing benefits. The program offers deliveries every two weeks valued at up to $250 each month directly to clients' doors, enabling homebound seniors to age in place. Requested funds will support staff hours and grocery costs to meet client needs.
3036.activities: Clients select from a list of groceries and household essentials, which are subsequently procured and delivered by personal shoppers. Personal shoppers conduct social worker check-ins with clients at each delivery and, when additional wrap-around services are needed, refer clients to a social worker or case manager for appropriate follow-up. Deliveries for individual clients will not exceed $125 per delivery and for 2 person households deliveries will not exceed $200 per delivery.
3036.direct_services: JCS Delivers provides: personalized grocery procurement for items beyond benefit coverage; bi-monthly home delivery ($250 max value per month); household essentials access; wellness checks during delivery; care coordination through social work/case management referrals. Services fill critical gaps for Home-Delivered Meals clients, supporting homebound seniors' nutritional needs and ability to age
3036.population: The target population is low income and/or homebound seniors assessed by a social worker to have a high nutrition risk scores.
3036.outcome: The goal of this project is to increase food security overall health and well-being for our most vulnerable seniors. Increased food security will be measured using the USDA Food insecurity Scale. An additional goal is to keep clients at home, and not reliant on government-funded residential care or hospitalization. During the client's initial assessment, their nutrition risk scores are documented and used as a baseline measurement. The clients are re-assessed annually, and they are given a food insecurity survey twice per year. The total number of groceries delivered and unduplicated client counts will be tracked monthly.

3342.description: Lake Jesup is a shallow nutrient impaired lake in Seminole County. Due to past alteration of its hydrologic connection to the St. John's River, decades of urban development, and accumulation of legacy nutrients in the sediments have led to continuous water quality degradation and chronic algal blooms that put human health, wildlife, recreation, and local economies at risk. Complementing past programs to reduce nutrient loading to the lake and current/future strategies to restore connectivity with the River and mitigate excess nutrients, particularly phosphorus, this project will inactivate 220,000 lbs of readily-available sediment phosphorus that will drastically improve water quality and reduce the occurrence of harmful algal blooms.
3342.purpose: Project will inactivate a significant portion of legacy phosphorus in Lake Jesup sediments and sequester new inputs from 3 key tributary creeks. This sequestration will dramatically improve the lake's water quality and clarity, reduce risk of harmful algal blooms and fish kills, and promote expansion of submersed vegetation to further stabilize restored water quality and improve habitat for fish and other wildlife. It will allow greater recreation and tourism for the benefit of local economies.
3342.activities: Funds will support a full-service contracted project through SJRWMD that includes final assessment of readily available legacy phosphorus in the sediments and post-treatment sediment phosphorus measurements on a quarterly- basis through 3 years post management
3342.direct_services: Rapid water quality improvement through direct mitigation of legacy phosphorus pollution in Lake Jesup will provide local citizens more effective use of Lake Jesup for fishing, hunting, and other recreation. It will also reduce risk of exposure to dissolved algal (or cyanobacterial) toxins in lake water through swimming or other recreational use, or via aerosolized toxins documented in association
3342.population: Approximately 550,000 residents live in Seminole County with continued residential and business development occurring in southern, western, and northern sections of the lake's watershed. Local and visiting fisherman and hunters utilize the lake, which in the past, was considered one of the best fishing lakes in Florida but that use has reduced.
3342.outcome: Sequestration of sediment phosphorus and a majority of new phosphorus inputs will improve water quality, reduce risk of harmful algal blooms, and increase water clarity. The management program will promote submersed aquatic vegetation, reduce risk of fish kills and shift the lake from a 'turbid state' to conditions promoting improved habitat, biodiversity and ecological function. The outcome will be directly measured through assessment of sediment phosphorus and lake water quality measurements already conducted by SJRWMD and augmented using automated measures proposed in this project.

3012.description: Supports individuals with disabilities and their families by providing coordinated services that promote stability, independence, & well-being. Through care coordination & case management, participants are connected to critical community resources & access to a 24/7 crisis line to address urgent needs. Services help close gaps in mental health & social services, reduce crises, & help families build self-sufficiency. The program advances community safety & resilience by actively combating antisemitism. Through education, awareness & community engagement, it equips participants, families, volunteers, and community partners with the tools to recognize, prevent, and respond to antisemitism and bias.
3012.purpose: The project equips people who have disabilities and their families with the tools, skills, and knowledge to overcome adversity and live full, productive lives. The care coordination & case management component connects families to vital community resources, targets mental health service gaps, provides a 24/7 crisis line, and builds self-sufficiency. Peer-mentoring and social activities develop social & emotional learning and daily living skills for children and adults.
3012.activities: Teen and adult mentors support children and adults with disabilities through recreational, athletic, and cultural activities while fostering inclusion, strengthening Jewish identity, and promoting awareness to combat antisemitism.
3012.direct_services: Case management provides counseling, resource referral, and community connections that foster inclusivity and acceptance of individuals with special needs and their families. Funding provides continuation of mental health & crisis line, as well as respite for parents/caretakers.
3012.population: The majority of the funds requested will serve elderly individuals; people with developmental and physical disabilities; individuals experiencing poor mental and physical health; and economically disadvantaged populations, with a particular focus on members of the Jewish community at large. The program will also support students across multiple age groups, including grade school, high school, and university/college students, ensuring services reach vulnerable individuals, families, and the broad
3012.outcome: The project will improve participants’ physical and mental health and enrich cultural connection by strengthening nutrition, daily living and independent functioning skills; increasing self-esteem, coping, and social belonging; and enhancing engagement in Jewish cultural and community life with safer access to programs and services. Outcomes will be measured through participant surveys, attendance and participation logs, data analysis, and direct observation, with health- and skill-related indicators tracked where applicable.

3434.description: Illegal cellphones in prisons fuel crimes, threaten staff, and endanger communities. Funding Tecore’s Managed Access System (MAS-E) will stop these communications at the source, protecting officers, victims, and families across Florida. MAS-E is not an optional technology; it is life-saving infrastructure essential to restoring safety and control inside Florida's correctional institutions.
3434.purpose: Illegal cellphones in prisons fuel crimes, threaten staff, and endanger communities. MAS-E is not an optional technology; it is life-saving infrastructure essential to restoring safety and control inside Florida's correctional institutions.
3434.activities: The funds will deploy Tecore’s MAS-E to Florida correctional facilities, providing secure communications across all cellular technologies, effectively operating as a controlled commercial carrier within the prison. Activities include blocking unauthorized inmate devices, facilitating authorized staff communications, automating intelligence gathering, and continuously monitoring the system to ensure institutional security and public safety.
3434.direct_services: The project directly protects citizens by preventing illegal inmate cellphone use that enables crime, extortion, and gang activity. MAS-E ensures correctional staff can maintain secure operations, reducing threats to communities, safeguarding families, and supporting public safety across Florida
3434.population: The target population includes all individuals impacted by criminal activity originating from Florida correctional facilities, including correctional staff, public safety officials, inmates, and the broader community. MAS-E will serve all 100,000+ inmates and 30,000+ staff across Florida’s state prisons.
3434.outcome: The project will prevent illegal inmate cellphone use, disrupt organized criminal enterprises operating from within correctional facilities, protect correctional staff, inmates, and the public, and improve overall institutional safety and control. Outcomes will be measured using MAS-E’s real-time dashboard analytics in addition to FDOC tracking measures, monitoring reductions in contraband communications, coordinated criminal incidents, staff assaults, and inmate infractions over time.

3215.description: Over 2,000 residents in the City of South Miami currently rely on outdated and malfunctioning septic systems that pose significant risks to public health, water quality, and the environment. A sub-area referred to as "Sub-area K" has been identified as a priority due to the threat of sea-level rise. Construction on Phase 1, which includes 46 homes and a building located in a City park, is being finalized. Funds are being requested for Phase 2 of the project, which would convert an additional 159 homes to a modern, efficient sewer system. With this project, we can improve sanitation, reduce pollution, and enhance overall quality of life for our community. Funding for this initiative will not only address these pressing issues but also create long-term cost savings by reducing maintenance and repair costs associated with aging septic infrastructure.
3215.purpose: With this project, we can improve sanitation, reduce pollution, and enhance overall quality of life for our community. Funding for this initiative will not only address these pressing issues but also create long-term cost savings by reducing maintenance and repair costs associated with aging septic infrastructure.
3215.activities: Construction services for Sub-area K Phase II of the sanitary sewer project
3215.direct_services: Citizens will receive a sanitary gravity sewer line to connect to in front of their home. This will give them the ability to abandon septic tanks and receive municipal sewer services.
3215.population: Individuals living in 159 homes in Phase 2 of Sub-Area K.
3215.outcome: The expected benefit of converting septic systems to a sewer system in a residential area is primarily to improve public health and environmental sustainability. By connecting homes to a centralized sewer system, the project aims to reduce the risk of septic system failures, which can lead to contamination of groundwater, surface water, and soil. This can also mitigate unpleasant odors and improve overall sanitation. Furthermore, the conversion will likely reduce maintenance costs for residents and improve the community's infrastructure, leading to better long-term outcomes for both health and property values.

3340.description: The City of Sunrise (City) has Fire Rescue Special Operations Units that are Broward County regional assets that respond to various emergencies on a county-wide basis. We are one of only four cities in Broward County that respond regionally to the entire county for hazmat. Since we respond to emergencies throughout the County it is critical that our Fire Rescue facilities are centrally located to respond as quickly as possible, especially for critical incidents. The City is seeking to build an additional fire rescue station, centrally located along Pine Island Road, near Oakland Park Boulevard. There are multiple potential opportunities to purchase land for a new Sunrise Fire Station in that area. The parameters for the new fire station include proximity to main roads for quick access, sufficient space for apparatuses, and the ability to serve our growing population and underserved areas

The pump station provides stormwater protection for critical facilities as well as many commercial and residential areas. There are operational issues with the current pump configuration and discharge from the station. Proposed improvements to the station will improve the operation and efficiency.

Situated on NW 2nd Street between NW 136th Avenue and International Parkway, it safeguards roughly 2,393 acres within Basin 8. The basin boundaries extend south to the North New River Canal, west to the South Florida Water Management District (SFWMD) L-35A Canal, north to Pat Salerno Drive, and east to Flamingo Road. Stormwater is discharged into the North New River Canal under the authority o
3341.activities: Construction of the upgrades of Stormwater Pump Station No. 8 include the replacement of all four pump and diesel drive units, modernization of the fuel storage and priming systems, electrical and structural rehabilitation, canal enhancements, installation of an automatic raker system, and construction of an upstream intermediate booster pump station.

3254.description: The college has a central HVAC plant including cooling towers, boilers, and plumbing that has been in place for 30 years and is on the verge of catastrophic failure which would close the entire Panama City Campus. The HVAC underground piping has been buried in a harsh environment for 30 years and the above ground cooling towers have also been exposed to harsh conditions as well. As a result of these environmental conditions and years of exposure to salt water, and being located at or near sea level, each of these systems has required constant maintenance and after years of use, replacement. Costs included are estimates and could vary due to market conditions at the time of construction. This project is survey recommended as 1.001 in the college's 2022 Educational Plant Survey.
3254.purpose: The specific purpose is to replace a 30 year old HVAC system now prone to repeated failures due to age and environmental factors which result in a total loss of cooling, heating and ventilation to the entire Panama City Campus when they occur.
3254.activities: The goal is to provide a comfortable and consistent environment, conducive to learning, for all students at the campus. Currently, the college has little control due to the frequent failures of the system.
3254.direct_services: The same direct services as in b. above will be provided to citizens by this project. Almost all of the college's students, faculty and staff are citizens of the college's service district, and the college is the host for many community events attended by area citizens.
3254.population: The primary target population is the approximately 8,000 students attending classes at any given time and 372 employees, but many others attend continuing education classes, theater productions, athletic events, and many other hosted community activities.
3254.outcome: The benefit of this project can be measured by operational time of the systems, number of failures and down time if any, and environmental satisfaction surveys.

3170.description: Franklin County (County) is requesting funds to purchase a Pumper/Tanker apparatus essential to the fire protection and public safety of the Alligator Point and St. Teresa communities. These areas lack dedicated water infrastructure, creating significant operational challenges for fire response. The Volunteer Fire Department currently does not have apparatus with the water capacity or pumping capability needed to sustain operations during large-scale fires. Without this equipment, the department’s ability to effectively respond to and contain major fire events is severely compromised, placing lives, property, and natural resources at risk.
3170.purpose: The requested funds will enable the Alligator Point / St. Teresa Volunteer Fire Department to acquire a specialized firefighting apparatus designed to provide a reliable and mobile water supply during emergency response operations. Without this capability, fire suppression efforts are severely hindered, particularly during large-scale wildfires and structural fires. The apparatus will enhance operational readiness, reduce response times, and significantly improve public safety for residents, vis
3170.activities: We will coordinate with the State Fire Marshal’s Office to establish deliverables and a procurement timeline for acquiring the pumper/tanker truck, leveraging our existing partnership to ensure compliance and efficient implementation.
3170.direct_services: This project will directly improve fire protection services for residents and visitors in Alligator Point and St. Teresa by ensuring timely access to water during emergencies. The new apparatus will enhance public safety, reduce property loss, and support faster, more effective response to wildfires, structure fires, and storm-related incidents.
3170.population: The apparatus will be housed at the Alligator Point / St Teresa Volunteer Fire Department (VFD). The targeted population will be the entire county to respond and support all the VFDs in Franklin County and the surrounding counties. The current population of Franklin County is 13,330 residents.
3170.outcome: The expected outcome is improved fire protection and emergency response capacity for Alligator Point and St. Teresa. This will be measured by reduced response times, increased water availability during incidents, and documented improvements in service coverage and readiness metrics reported by the Volunteer Fire Department.

3386.description: The Five STAR Veterans Center helps homeless or displaced veterans who are suffering with Post Traumatic Stress or other behavioral health issues. The goal is to achieve greater self-determination, independent living, increased financial stability, and improved job skills through an individual Passport to Independence long-term goal achievement plan to help with re-integration to civilian life.
3386.purpose: The Five STAR Veterans Center helps homeless or displaced veterans who are suffering with Post Traumatic Stress or other behavioral health issues. The goal is to achieve greater self-determination, independent living, increased financial stability, and improved job skills through an individual Passport to Independence long-term goal achievement plan to help with re-integration to civilian life.
3386.activities: Five Star Veteran Center is Northeast Florida's only veteran housing community for homeless or displaced veterans, and the first facility in Florida that focuses solely on our veterans in need. The Passport to Independence program is a full wrap around program catering to veterans individual needs to re-integrate to civilian life.
3386.direct_services: Five Star Veterans Center provides evidence-based treatment methods focused on helping to develop solid strategies to promote healthy decision making and to heal emotional/psychological distress of participants. Administer random urine drug and alcohol screens to residents.
3386.population: Persons with poor mental and/or physical health, jobless and economically disadvantaged persons, homeless, drug users and/or offenders, currently or formerly incarcerated persons, and veterans. The Center is currently able to house approximately 40 veterans at a time.
3386.outcome: Improve physical and mental health, enhance economic self-sufficiency, reduce recidivism and substance abuse, and divert from the criminal and juvenile justice system. Pre and Post program evaluations will be used to measure the outcomes.

3429.organization: Life Management Center of Northwest Florida,
3429.description: The Circuit 14 Central Receiving Facility (CRF) provides children and adults in the 6 counties of Circuit 14 with centralized 24/7 access to behavioral health crisis evaluation and intervention services. The CRF will provide a single point of access for law enforcement, hospital E.R.'s, and first responders to refer those requiring voluntary or involuntary evaluation and stabilization consistent with the Baker Act or Marchman Act. Persons at the CRF will be more efficiently and effectively referred to outpatient treatment or service agencies at their discretion. The CRF is a statewide model, and there are no such facilities within Circuit 14.
3429.purpose: The Circuit 14 Central Receiving Facility (CRF) will provide children and adults in the 6 counties of Circuit 14 with centralized 24/7 access to behavioral health crisis evaluation and intervention services. This service will also provide a single point of access for law enforcement, hospital emergency rooms, and first responders to refer persons requiring immediate voluntary or involuntary evaluation and/or stabilization consistent with the Baker Act or Marchman Act.
3429.activities: The Central Receiving Facility will establish a "no wrong door" approach for Circuit 14 residents in need of urgent crisis behavioral health services, coordinated and transitional outpatient care, referral services, and medication management.
3429.direct_services: CRF will establish a single point of access for residents in need of crisis services and a central location for local law enforcement, area hospitals/emergency departments, other designated receiving facilities, first responders, and the Circuit Judicial Court system to refer persons for voluntary or involuntary psychiatric inpatient services consistent with the Baker Act and Marchman Act.
3429.population: Individuals in need of evaluation and/or stabilization under the Baker Act or Marchman Act. Over 800 children and adults will be served.
3429.outcome: Referral, evaluation, facilitation of outpatient and inpatient services. This state-wide model facilitates the efficient use of resources and provides a central location for law enforcement, hospital, emergency depts., receiving facilities, first responders, and the Circuit Judicial Courts to refer persons to voluntary/involuntary inpatient services consistent with the Baker Act and the Marchman Act. Evidence based tools and data collection will be used to demonstrate benefits/outcomes. Managing Entity/DCF reports will be consistent with all requirements.

3524.organization: Life Management Center of Northwest Florida,
3524.description: In Fiscal Year 2024-25, 146 children and adolescents were referred to other long-distance Florida Baker Act inpatient providers due to lack of such "bed space" with the two Circuit 14 providers. The purpose and goal of the present funding request is to provide additional staffing for Life Management Center to expand Baker Act inpatient services to youth under age 18 in a facility that can treat them in closer proximity to their homes and community.
3524.purpose: Provide added "bed space" at Life Management Center to serve individuals under the age of 18 with necessary Baker Act inpatient services within and closest to their home communities. In Fiscal Year 2024-25, 146 minors were referred to other long distance Florida Baker Act inpatient providers due to lack of bed space in Circuit 14. This change will also facilitate parental and family involvement for effective discharge plans and treatment.
3524.activities: Added psychiatric evaluation and assessment of individuals meeting Baker Act criteria who are voluntarily or involuntarily arriving at Life Management Center will be more effectively assessed and admitted to inpatient treatment services as indicated, instead of being transferred 100 or more miles outside of Circuit 14.
3524.direct_services: Psychiatric evaluation and treatment services will be provided on an inpatient basis for children and adolescents. Medication management to stabilize serious psychiatric illnesses with minors will be provided. Discharge planning will include continued outpatient evaluation and treatment services as indicated. Increased family and caregiver involvement will be facilitated.
3524.population: The target population to be served will include persons under 18 years of age who are having serious mental health issues and who are exhibiting the potential for harming others or risk for suicide and self-harm. At least 100 children and adolescents and their families, guardians, or care providers will be served by this project.
3524.outcome: This project will serve children and adolescents who are currently referred to inpatient psychiatric facilities outside of Bay County. Transfer of these children can include travel of over 100 miles from their home communities. Treating children and adolescents with this project will eliminate unnecessary and added adjustments for these children and their families with the least amount of additional disruption to their adjustment. Effective discharge planning will be completed to facilitate increased and ongoing outpatient treatment.

3518.description: Bridgeway Center, Inc. respectfully requests local funding in the amount of $15,000 to enhance access to essential medications, treatment, and supportive services for uninsured and low-income residents in Okaloosa County. This funding supports individuals reentering the community following incarceration through coordinated transition planning and support services. This initiative aims to reduce financial barriers, strengthen treatment engagement, and promote recovery for individuals facing mental health and substance use challenges.
3518.purpose: To eliminate financial barriers for low-income individuals in need of medications, lab testing, and behavioral health services related to mental health, substance use, or co-occurring conditions, ensuring equitable access to comprehensive care and recovery support.
3518.activities: To support individuals with mental health, substance use, or co-occurring disorders by combining FDA-approved medications (e.g., buprenorphine, naltrexone) with counseling and behavioral therapies, improving recovery outcomes and reducing relapse and overdose rates.
3518.direct_services: The $15,000 in funding supports individuals in Bridgeway services by providing medical assessments, medication management, counseling, peer support, and partial coverage of treatment medications. Funding reduces barriers to care through tools like transportation to appointments, helping individuals stay in treatment, reduce substance use, pursuing recovery, and lower relapse and recidivism rates.
3518.population: All funding will support indigent behavioral health services and Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) for residents in and around Okaloosa County. Target populations include individuals facing mental or physical health challenges, unemployment, economic hardship, homelessness, or justice involvement due to substance use. The project also assists individuals reentering the community after incarceration through coordinated transition planning and support services, ensuring access to critical care f
3518.outcome: The benefit expectations are improved physical and mental health, a reduction in overdose deaths, and promotion of long-term recovery and self-sufficiency through expanded access to treatment and medicated assisted care. Outcomes will be measured by treatment retention rates, reduction in relapse, recidivism, and emergency room visits/hospitalizations, and increased employment and housing stability among participants.

3079.description: The City of Opa-locka seeks to transform Ingram Park into a premier multi-purpose sports hub, anchored by a state-of- the-art synthetic turf football/soccer field and an eight-lane running track. Team rooms/restroom building refresh, small storage/concessions, shade structures, expanded parking/wayfinding, security/CCTV, and landscape gateways. The City has chosen to develop Ingram Park into a sports hub facility due to the following factors: Strategic location: Centrally located with easy access to schools, neighborhoods, and the Tri-Rail station. Community demand: High youth participation in football, soccer, and track with no comparable facility nearby. Equity impact: Opa-locka is a historically underserved community where investment will have outsized benefits.
3079.purpose: The purpose of these funds would be to provide restore working recreational infrastructure, that the City would not otherwise reasonably be able to afford to replace at the time it was damaged.
3079.activities: The City will contract with a several providers to replace old and damaged recreational infrastructure and add new facilities. Transform Ingram Park into a premier multi-purpose sports hub, anchored by a state-of-the-art synthetic turf football/soccer field and an eight-lane running track. synthetic-turf football/soccer multi-purpose field (2-in-1 striping), 8- lane track resurfacing/installation, Musco-type sports lighting, video scoreboard/sound, player areas, fencing, site drainage upgrades,
3079.direct_services: The administration of a municipal recreational program with a high participation rate.
3079.population: City of Opa-locka residents, and visitors. Roughly 800 individuals or more are expected to be served.
3079.outcome: This project will provide recreational opportunities to under served children and young adults in Opa-locka and surrounding areas. It is commonly known that a tight knit community with significant parental involvement leads to better outcomes for children and young adults. The City is able to record the number of participants in community sports. The City expects a quick increase of participants in community sports activities upon completion of this project. This can be recorded.

3618.description: The requested funding amount will be used to reimburse child welfare provider agencies who were not paid by Embrace Families prior to their contact with the DCF being withdrawn. These agencies have performed child welfare services, as a contract provider on behalf of the State of Florida, and are owed these funds.
3618.purpose: Support Abused, Abandoned, and neglected children
3618.activities: These funds will be used to reimburse agencies for services that have already been provided to vulnerable children and families, who are/were being served through the child welfare system during Embrace Families contract period.
3618.direct_services: Reimbursement for services already provided to vulnerable children and families.
3618.population: Youth, At-Risk Youth, Abused, Abandoned, and neglected children.
3618.outcome: The expenditure of funds requested will be used to reimburse child welfare providers agencies who provided child welfare services on behalf of the State of Florida. Unpaid services has resulted in a shortfall in the budgets of these provider agencies, having a negative fiscal impact on their agency, impacting their ability to continue to provider services to children in foster care.

3174.description: This request is for continuation funding of a statewide DEP administered grants program from the Federal Grants Trust Fund (not General Revenue) which allows publicly owned utilities to remove sand and grit from wastewater treatment plants and associated collection systems which remain in operation. Distribution is on a first-come, first-serve basis with local matches, except that waiver of the match is allowed for publicly owned and utilities in rural counties,and impoverished counties and municipalities.
3174.purpose: Sand and Grit Removal Grants for Wastewater Treatment Facilities. This request is for continuation funding of a statewide DEP administered grants program from the Federal Grants Trust Fund (not General Revenue) which allows publicly owned utilities to remove sand and grit from wastewater treatment plants and associated collection systems which remain in operation. Distribution is on a first-come, first-serve basis with focus on rural counties,and impoverished counties and municipalities.
3174.activities: Clean hard-to-reach environments in wastewater collection and treatment systems saving municipalities time and energy costs by maintaining facilities instead of replacing infrastructure.
3174.direct_services: Restored wastewater treatment facility capacity and reduced energy costs.
3174.population: All citizens who create wastewater must receive wastewater treatment; many thousands.
3174.outcome: Restored wastewater treatment facility capacity and reduced energy costs. Outcome is difficult to measure, but there is very significant savings due to the relatively low cost of capacity restoration from clean-out versus construction of new facilities.

3098.description: The American History Live program is a free resource for all Florida educators to help students retain American history and civics knowledge. Our purpose is to encourage young Florida students to become responsible, informed citizens. Our animated historical characters, featuring trained voice-over talent, include Benjamin Franklin, Abigail Adams, Prince Hall, Alexander Hamilton, and Betsy Ross. Lessons focus on early American history, the founding documents, and civics.
3098.purpose: To provide Florida educators with a unique interactive tool for K-12th grade instruction and retention of American history and civics. Our program meets Florida State Academic Standards in Social Studies, including lessons on Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, and the founding documents. The program, including our Prince Hall character, covers Florida African American history standards. Our program can be used to help prepare students for the 7th-grade End-of-Course Civics Assessment and age
3098.activities: Educators are provided with live, interactive lessons conducted by animated characters Benjamin Franklin, Abigail Adams, Prince Hall, Alexander Hamilton, and Betsy Ross, with trained voice-over talent, to engage students in history and civics lessons. Utilizing a secure video-conference platform, the program is available in all 67 counties. Educators are provided with a lesson plan, a complete script, and multiple assessment options. They are encouraged to collaborate with our curriculum special
3098.direct_services: All Florida educators will have access to American History Live at no cost. Our program is available to public schools, charter schools, homeschoolers, private schools, and community centers. Educators utilize the program as a single historical visit or a multi-lesson unit plan. Every citizen can access our videos and unique interactive programs. All lessons and scripts are available to Florida re
3098.population: The target population consists of K-8th-grade students in both traditional and non-traditional schools in Florida. We expect to serve over 5,000 students in live, interactive lessons with the funding requested. Our Prince Hall and African American history videos can also be used as a tool for high school educators to meet new African American history standards. Our program aims to reach all students, including those who are pulled from Social Studies instruction to receive additional support in
3098.outcome: Program's expected benefit is providing educators with an additional tool to prepare K-7th-grade students for the cumulative 7th-grade End-of-Course Civics Assessment. The method used to measure our program's success will be a pre- and post-assessment of students, offered to educators, to evaluate retention when our program is utilized. Educators will be provided with multiple follow-up activities to meet the needs of their students. Our program is not meant only to pass exams, but to allow all students to engage with American History.

3099.organization: Tampa Museum of Art Foundation Inc.
3099.description: The TMA's collection of over 8,000 works is used as a springboard for education programs of Modern, Contemporary and Greek, Roman and Etruscan art serving students in primary, secondary and higher education institutions, as well as adults and life-long learners of all ages. Its classical antiquities collection -- originally purchased with financial commitment from the State of Florida, Hillsborough County, and the City of Tampa and matched with support from individual gifts across the region -- inspires exhibitions, artistic creation and reflection on the tenets of Western Civilization, Democracy, Civics and the Classics. State funding of $1.5 million will support the museum's expansion and site redevelopment, a multi-faceted Downtown Tampa Project designed to revitalize the waterfront and address blight in the region. The state's contribution will help to triple the museum's education a
3099.purpose: The TMA seeks funds toward a $128 million dollar expansion to strengthen its working capital and operating budget with the goal of expanding its serving capacity and enhancing its community impact. The TMA's collection of over 8,000 works is used as a springboard for education programs of Modern, Contemporary and Greek, Roman and Etruscan art. It is also leveraged to expand access and bring borrowed private and public collections to the museum to inspire reflection on the tenets of Western Civil
3099.activities: The museum's collections and community engagement programs have developed as community partnerships with over 300 organizations in Florida – including 197 K-12 schools, 10 colleges and universities, 49 community organizations; 18 senior groups and 13 youth groups -- to deliver state-of-the-art educational programs that provide a unique and invaluable resource for Florida students across the state, both in person and through the museum's virtual collection, to learn firsthand from these irreplace
3099.direct_services: TMA will provide: school tours to 40,000 K-12 students and serve 14,000 children and adults through 160+ onsite education programs, 200 offsite classes and events and year-round educational activities; free general admission to college students, active military and veterans year-round; provide over 100 unique three-hour classes affiliated with 17 county-wide agencies focused on mental health throu
3099.population: TMA expects to serve over 165,000 individuals by 2028 as a result of the expansion project. Target populations include grade school, high school and preschool students; University/College Students; aging populations; persons with poor mental health; persons with poor physical health; economically disadvantaged persons; at-risk youth; homeless; physically disabled; drug users (in health services); general public, local community and tourists. In addition to contributing to community revitalizatio
3099.outcome: The following benefits/outcomes are expected: Improve quality of education (measure: benchmark assessment of improved performance of students via Hillsborough County Schools and statewide); Improve mental health (measure: participant surveys and attendance); Enrich cultural experience (measure: increased attendance from minority, majority, and economically disadvantaged zip code regions); Increase/Improve economic activity (measure: TMA increase in revenue); Increase Tourism (measure: Zip code data for increased visitors); Create job opportunities (measure: positions filled for construction, contractors, and programming. expansion).

3100.description: This initiative will pilot an AI-powered support solution to assist with non-emergency call management and related operational workflows. The program is designed to improve response efficiency, reduce dispatcher workload, and enhance community engagement. Both teams will collaborate on data analysis, workflow design, and implementation planning to ensure effective deployment and measurable operational impact.
3100.purpose: This initiative will pilot an AI-powered support solution to assist with non-emergency call management and related operational workflows. The program is designed to improve response efficiency, reduce dispatcher workload, and enhance community engagement. Both teams will collaborate on data analysis, workflow design, and implementation planning to ensure effective deployment and measurable operational impact.
3100.activities: Answering non-emergency calls that come into from citizens, documentation and call forwarding/routing as necessary.
3100.direct_services: Answering non-emergency calls that come into from citizens, documentation and call forwarding/routing as necessary.
3100.population: Elderly persons Persons with poor mental health Persons with poor physical health Jobless persons Economically disadvantaged persons At-risk youth Homeless Developmentally disabled Physically disabled The entire population will be served
3100.outcome: The project will improve public safety by ensuring emergency dispatchers are available to respond to true emergencies rather than being occupied with non-emergency calls. The level of benefit will be measured by the reduction in dispatcher time spent on non-emergency calls and the decrease in average response times for emergency incidents, tracked through call-handling and dispatch performance metrics.

3296.description: Fernandina Beach is a 200-year-old city located on Amelia Island between the Atlantic Ocean and the Amelia River. The City's Downtown Historic District consists of a flourishing commercial district bustling with shops, restaurants, breweries, cultural sites, and 60 blocks of expertly preserved Victorian-era homes. In 2024, 78.7% (815,174) of Amelia Island's 1,035,800 visitors ranked the Historic District as a "Top Activity Enjoyed," scoring higher than even the Island's beaches. The Fernandina Beach Historic District borders the Amelia River which periodically and with growing frequency overflows onto downtown streets, flooding the railroad and the Port. Storms, and even heavy rain now creates standing bodies of water throughout the Historic District. A new state appropriation of $4,000,000 will fund an additional 223 linear feet of the seawall, increasing the construction completion fro
3296.purpose: Travel publications consistently rank Amelia Island one of best island and beach destinations in the U.S. In 2023, Amelia Island tourism contributed over $1.2 billion in economic impact, employed over 25% of Nassau County, FL residents, and provided almost $453 million in wages to Amelia Island employees. Historic Downtown Fernandina Beach, a business and residential district populated with Victorian-aged business structures and homes, was ranked a favorite activity by 78.7% of Amelia Island vis

Beyond annual seasonal tourism, Fernandina Beach hosts recurring cultural events and festivals that bring hundreds of thousands of additional visitors - and tourism r

3411.organization: Family Support Services of North Florida
3411.description: This investment will align with the Fostering the Future executive order and replace previous contract-based funding that is no longer available due to rising costs of care. We aim to enhance life-skills and employment-readiness support for older youth who are aging out, or have already aged out, of foster care. The support will strengthen key programs all under the signature program Bridge to Work, which prepares youth aging out of care with employability and self- sufficiency skills.
3411.purpose: This programming aims to enhance the life-skills and employment-readiness support for older foster youth. The support will strengthen key programs all under the signature program Bridge to Work, which prepares youth aging out of care with employability and self-sufficiency skills.
3411.activities: Just Like Me - therapeutic arts camp that utilizes the arts as a tool for expression Bridge to Work - program to teach work skills and career progression The Challenge - program that enhances skills needed for real-world success and independence SPLASH - a water-safety/lifeguard-certification pathway
3411.direct_services: Programming is focused on the oder youth and provides direct supports that include an arts-based therapeutic camp fostering healthy expression, hands-on workforce training that builds job readiness and career momentum, practical life-skills instruction that equips youth for everyday independence, and a water-safety and lifeguard certification track that offers both skill development and employment
3411.population: The target population for this project is older foster youth who are aging out, or have already aged out, of foster care. We are expecting to serve approximately 250 youth.
3411.outcome: Youth show measurable gains in emotional wellness, job readiness, independent living skills, and safety certification. Program impact is supported by documented completion rates, skill mastery assessments, and employment or credential attainment. Additionally, the National Youth in Transition Database screening tool is used to assess impact of provided services.

3337.description: The project involves replacement of the sanitary sewer collection system at Ixora Park (9,700 linear feet of vitrified clay pipe) that has reached the end of its service life. The county inherited this 1959 sewer collection system about 20 years ago. Frequent failures of the system result in sinkholes in the community's roadways, presenting a public safety hazard and service interruptions. Because of the pipe's location adjacent to the south relief canal, a failure could result in sewage flowing to the Indian River Lagoon. Since 2016, there have been 109 work orders to repair the system and/or road.
3337.purpose: The project includes replacing the sanitary sewer collection system (9,700 linear feet of vitrified clay pipe) at Ixora Park that has reached the end of its service life. The goals include reducing road damage and reducing SSOs into South Relief Canal and minimize the risk that untreated wastewater will reach the Indian River Lagoon (IRL). This project will improve water quality and assist the county in meeting it's water quality requirements under the IRL Basin Management Action Plan.
3337.activities: Replace the sanitary sewer collection system, which is 9,700 linear feet of vitrified clay pipe
3337.direct_services: The project provides a more reliable wastewater system that reduces the need for work order repairs to the sewer system and the road. This project also will improve water quality in the adjacent waterways because of reduced sanitary sewer overflows.
3337.population: This is the main sewer main that serves the Ixora Park Subdivision with 275 homes.
3337.outcome: Reduced number of work order repair requests - track the number of work orders to measure the outcome

3332.description: Improve the capacity of the Davis St culvert to reduce flooding potential and provide resiliency from sea level rise for State Road A1A, the Neptune Beach Central Business District, and residential properties in the most densely populated area of the City of Neptune Beach.
3332.purpose: Improve the capacity of the Davis St culvert to reduce flooding potential and provide resiliency from sea level rise for State Road A1A, the Neptune Beach Central Business District, and residential properties in the most densely populated area of the City of Neptune Beach.
3332.activities: Construction of culvert and drainage enhancements.
3332.direct_services: Reduction in flooding and potential property damage.
3332.population: Over 50% of Neptune Beach residents and businesses are at risk in the impacted drainage basin. Entire population of Neptune Beach (7,088) would be served as this basin encompasses the City's primary commercial district.
3332.outcome: Reduce flood stages located upstream. Measurement of flood stage improvements for 25 year, 50 year and 100 year and 24 hour simulations.

3061.organization: Jessie Trice Community Health Systems, Inc.
3061.description: "Home 1st" enables aging-in-place through PACE partnerships and FQHC integration, expanding services like home- based and in-house medical, dental, behavioral health, physical therapy, and exercise programs. Care delivery is improved through professional and interdisciplinary training for CHWs, family medicine providers, and residents, enhancing outcomes and reducing costly institutional care.
3061.purpose: Home 1st" enables aging-in-place through PACE partnerships and FQHC integration, expanding services like home- based and in-house medical, dental, behavioral health, physical therapy, and exercise programs. Care delivery is improved through professional and interdisciplinary training for CHWs, family medicine providers, and residents, enhancing outcomes and reducing costly institutional care.
3061.activities: This program will strengthen care for geriatric and veteran populations through a coordinated, inter-professional team model that delivers integrated medical, behavioral health, dental and social services to improve overall outcomes at our FQHC sites, a PACE Center(s) and through home visitations for persons 65 and older and for veterans.
3061.direct_services: Direct services include home, clinic, or PACE center visits, telehealth, physical therapy, 4Ms assessments, medication review, exercise and nutrition counseling, and screenings for non-medical needs such as housing, legal support, and food security, delivered with care coordination by case managers and community health workers.
3061.population: The target population are elderly persons, persons with poor mental and physical health, economically disadvantaged persons, homeless, developmentally and physically disabled. Between 201-400 individuals are expected to be served.
3061.outcome: Improve Physical Health for seniors by regularly tracking assessments such as mobility; fall risk; DEXA scan results and remote patient monitoring. Improve mental health for participants by monitoring depressive symptoms and providing structured exercise and PT sessions. This can be measured by 9 question evidence-based screening tool. Enrich cultural experience by integrating culturally relevant elements such as music, language and traditions. Improve quality of education for geriatric patients by providing structured training and certificates.

The homelessness services program is designed to support individuals by providing access to essentials, case management, workforce development, use of address and daily access to the facility. We operate a free and charitable clinic that serves uninsured residents of Duval County, providing primary care, prescriptive medication and nutritious food, and integrated behavioral health. This funding would help Mission House continue to serve our 650 clients/patients per year, while continuing efforts to expand mental health services.
3413.purpose: The specific purpose of this funding is to provide the resources to staff to provide the programming and mental health program for our clients and patients of Mission House. By utilizing these funds to increase access to case management, workforce development and mental health services, it helps provide a hand up to the street homeless and working poor of Duval and northern St. John's Counties. By providing this funding, an avenue to self-sufficiency is provided to our clients and patients who r
3413.activities: Funds will support trained staff who conduct client/patient intake, case planning, benefits navigation, clinical visits, mental health screenings, and ongoing follow-up. Staff ensure daily operations are managed effectively, safely, and in compliance with regulations. The mental health counselor would be free of charge to clients and patients enrolled in the programs.

3413.outcome: The benefits include providing case management services to lead to better life outcomes (referral to substance abuse treatment, help with job placement, clean clothes and meals) and will be measured by the number of clients served annually. For the clinic side, the goal is to serve 300 people each year providing 50 visits per month. Success will be measured by amount of patient visits each year. 3598.description: The Ronald McDonald House Charities of Jacksonville (RMHC JAX) is at full capacity as pediatric care grows across Wolfson Children’s, UF Proton, Nemours, Brooks Rehabilitation and soon Mayo Clinic’s ion carbon therapy. With rising oncology demand and long family stays, we must expand. State support for a $500,000 feasibility study will guide the best path forward so no family is turned away during their child’s medical crisis.
3598.purpose: A feasibility study will assess projected pediatric demand, analyze partner growth, determine required expansion size and cost, evaluate community financial support, and provide a clear plan to ensure Florida families have needed lodging and support during their child’s medical care.
3598.activities: The study will inform expansion of family lodging that supports children’s access to consistent, uninterrupted medical care, improving adherence to treatment plans and overall health outcomes, Enhance specific individual’s economic self sufficiency, Reduce substance abuse.
3598.direct_services: The study will inform expansion of family lodging that supports children’s access to consistent, uninterrupted medical care, improving adherence to treatment plans and overall health outcomes.
3598.population: Persons with poor mental health, Persons with poor physical health, Jobless persons, Economically disadvantaged persons, Developmentally disabled, Physically disabled, Preschool students, Grade school students, High school students, University/College students, Victims of crime, Pediatric patients and their families.
3598.outcome: The study will inform expansion of family lodging that supports children’s access to consistent, uninterrupted medical care, improving adherence to treatment plans and overall health outcomes. Post-expansion, physical health outcomes will be measured through hospital partner data on treatment completion rates for families utilizing Ronald McDonald House services. Expanded lodging capacity will help reduce family stress and anxiety by keeping parents close to their hospitalized children during treatment. Impact will be evaluated through family satisfaction surveys and comparison of pre/post-expansion family wellbeing data. While the feasibility study will not directly impact education, improv

3376.description: Funds will assist the construction of the Florida Dyslexia Literacy Center, where teachers from around Florida can learn the Orton-Gillingham method, a multi-sensory and data-driven approach to teaching the dyslexic brain. All kids can learn with this method; dyslexic kids can ONLY learn with this method. With 20% of the population being dyslexic, this Literacy Center will be instrumental for teachers, parents and students across Florida.
3376.purpose: The funds will construct the Florida Dyslexia Literacy Center where teachers from across Florida can learn the Orton- Gillingham method, a multisensory and data-driven approach to teach students with dyslexia. This facility will provide training, resources, and support to improve literacy outcomes statewide.
3376.activities: The center will offer professional development workshops and certification courses in the Orton-Gillingham method for educators, provide instructional materials and resources, host family education sessions, and support outreach programs to schools and communities to promote evidence-based dyslexia interventions.
3376.direct_services: Citizens will receive access to specialized literacy instruction and intervention services for students with dyslexia, educator training programs, parent workshops, and community outreach events that provide strategies for supporting dyslexic learners.
3376.population: The project serves teachers, parents, and students impacted by dyslexia throughout Florida. With approximately 20% of the population affected by dyslexia, the center expects to train hundreds of educators annually and indirectly benefit thousands of students and their families statewide.
3376.outcome: The project is expected to significantly improve reading proficiency and literacy outcomes for students with dyslexia by equipping educators with evidence-based instructional methods and expanding access to specialized interventions. Outcomes will be measured by tracking the number of teachers trained and certified, the number of students receiving services, and quantitative improvements in reading scores and progress monitoring assessments before and after participation.

3361.description: Funds will support design, permitting, system evaluation, and preliminary engineering for process control and monitoring upgrades at the City’s wastewater treatment facility. These improvements will provide real-time monitoring of system conditions to optimize treatment efficiency and effluent quality, supporting corrective actions under FDEP Consent Order OGC No. 25-1664 and advancing nutrient-reduction goals within the Lower St. Johns River Main Stem BMAP and Crescent Lake.
3361.purpose: Funds will support design, permitting, system evaluation, and preliminary engineering for process control and monitoring upgrades at the City’s wastewater treatment facility. These improvements will support real-time monitoring to optimize treatment efficiency and effluent quality, supporting corrective actions under FDEP Consent Order OGC No. 25-1664 and advancing nutrient-reduction goals within the Lower St. Johns River Main Stem BMAP and Crescent Lake.
3361.activities: The project will include design, permitting, system evaluation, and preliminary engineering for advanced process controls, instrumentation, and monitoring equipment. Work will improve automation, treatment process control, and data collection, providing operators with accurate, continuous feedback to maintain compliance and optimize performance.
3361.direct_services: The project will protect public health and the environment by ensuring high-quality wastewater treatment and reliable facility operation. Residents and visitors will benefit from cleaner receiving waters used for recreation and reduced risk of sanitary system failures or permit violations that could affect the community.
3361.population: The project will directly serve the City of Crescent City’s approximately 1,700 residents, as well as local businesses, schools, and critical facilities. The benefits extend to residents and visitors throughout the Lower St. Johns River Basin who rely on local waterways for recreation and tourism.
3361.outcome: The project will improve treatment efficiency. Success will be measured through improved effluent quality.

3363.description: The funds will support the design and permitting of the replacement and extension of approximately 6,300 feet of aging water mains along Lake St, Palm Ave, Central Ave, Cypress Ave, Park St, and Florida Ave. It will improve water pressure, reliability, and fire protection while connecting all parcels along the route to the new system and abandoning the failing infrastructure. These upgrades will ensure safe, consistent water service for residents and businesses while reducing operational and maintenance issues.
3363.purpose: The funds will be used to complete design, survey, geotechnical investigation, permitting, and related engineering services needed to advance the Lake Street & South Tower Water Main Improvements project to a shovel-ready status. This work will prepare the City for future construction by producing engineered drawings, permit applications, and bid-ready documents.
3363.activities: Activities include topographic surveying, geotechnical borings and analysis, engineering design of the proposed water main replacement and extensions, coordination with utilities, preparation of construction documents, cost estimating, and securing all required FDEP and local permits. These services will position the City to competitively bid the project for construction.
3363.direct_services: The project will provide direct services to citizens by ensuring a more reliable and efficient water distribution system, improving water pressure, and enhancing fire flow capabilities. It will replace outdated infrastructure, reducing the likelihood of water service disruptions or system failures. Residents and businesses will benefit from increased water reliability for daily needs, improved fir
3363.population: The target population served by this project includes the ˜1,700 residents of Crescent City, Florida. The project will provide these individuals with increased water pressure and an additional volume of water for fire flow, enhancing both daily water reliability and the community's ability to respond to fire emergencies effectively.
3363.outcome: The expected outcome of this request is the completion of all engineering, survey, geotechnical, and permitting tasks required to make the project shovel-ready. Once constructed, the overall project will increase potable water pressure, enhance fire flow capacity, and improve system reliability for Crescent City. The design-phase outcome will be measured by the delivery of bid-ready construction documents, approved permits, and completed technical reports; construction-phase outcomes will be measured by comparing pre- and post-project water pressure and fire flow data.

3146.description: Growing USF's initiatives that bolster national & critical infrastructure security thru USF's Global & National Security Institute, Institute for Applied Engineering, Cyber FL, Bellini College of AI, Cybersecurity & Computing and other related initiatives. As part of BOG's State University System (SUS) 30 Strategic Plan, 2 of USF's 3 BOG-approved "areas of expertise" are Human & Infrastructure Security and Applied AI. The funds will support the growth of USF's efforts to contribute to long-term SUS goals in those areas.
3146.purpose: Expand USF ’s human and infrastructure security disciplines and institutes at USF such as Global and National Security Institute, Institute of Applied Engineering, and other related programs and centers and by doing so, increase partnership agreements with entities engaged in national security such as MacDill AFB, CENTCOM, SOCOM, DOD, Army Research Labs, and others.
3146.activities: USF is home to a rare and distinctive program that immerses students in the world of intelligence and national security and Tampa is uniquely positioned as a hub for national security with MacDill Air Force Base. The funding will help build a national security talent pipeline through innovative programs and public and private cyber and military partnerships.
3146.direct_services: Through academic programs, internships and fellowships, the funding will help expand programs to offer students and active duty and military veterans direct pathways into careers with the CIA, FBI, State Department, military intelligence and leading defense contractors and shape the future of Florida’s national security workforce while further positioning Tampa Bay as a leader in intelligence and
3146.population: University students and US Military and Homeland defense. Approximately 400 individuals are expected to be served.
3146.outcome: Improve quality of education: Improve opportunities for students to work on national security challenges and prepare the next generation of homeland security professionals. Student enrollments in, and completion of, programs of strategic emphasis with ties to national security. Protect the general public from harm: Develop additional and expanded applied research partnerships with national security practitioners in Florida and nationally. Number of agreements executed and productivity and ROI from those agreements.

3378.description: Clearing and grading sites for immediate development is essential to build a competitive life sciences ecosystem in Pasco, Greater Tampa, and across Florida. A $5M state investment would unlock 25 acres in the heart of our campus for development. Private developers and companies will then invest their own capital to construct on the prioritized site. We project this will create roughly 500 construction jobs and 1,875 permanent jobs by 2032.
3378.purpose: The development that will occur on these sites will be accretive to the prevention and cure of cancer using next- generation modalities. This will aid more than 50,000 Florida families who lose a loved one to cancer each year.
3378.activities: Use of next-generation modalities for cancer treatment.
3378.direct_services: At Speros, we estimate unlocking ~25 acres for development would create 1875 jobs and lead to $23M in future state and local tax revenue. This would also deepen a growing focus for Florida by investing in the bio and life sciences cluster. Clearing and grading sites will lead to more than 500 construction jobs over the next five years and pave the way for ~1875 permanent jobs.
3378.population: Families in Citrus, Hernando, Hillsborough, and Pasco counties. Estimated 50,000 Florida families a year.
3378.outcome: Expected benefit to come of this project is the prevention and cure of cancer using next-generation modalities measured by future data on treatment outcomes.

3589.description: The City of Homestead requests state funding for the construction of a police substation on the east side of the City to enhance public safety, improve response times, and expand law enforcement presence in an area experiencing continued residential and commercial growth. The proposed facility will support community policing efforts, decentralized patrol operations, and improved access to police services for residents and businesses located east of the Florida Turnpike. The substation will allow officers to be deployed closer to service areas, improving operational efficiency and visibility within the community.
3589.purpose: The purpose of the funding is to construct a police substation that strengthens law enforcement capacity on the east side of the City, reduces emergency and non-emergency response times, enhances patrol efficiency, and supports community-oriented policing strategies.
3589.activities: The facility will support patrol deployment, report-taking, investigative support, community outreach activities, and daily police operations. Officers assigned to the substation will provide direct law enforcement services, traffic enforcement, neighborhood patrols, and increased engagement with residents and businesses in the surrounding area.
3589.direct_services: Citizens will receive improved access to police services, faster response times, increased patrol presence, and enhanced public safety coverage within the east side of Homestead.
3589.population: The project will serve residents, businesses, and visitors located on the east side of the City of Homestead, benefiting tens of thousands of individuals through improved public safety services and law enforcement accessibility.
3589.outcome: Outcomes will be measured through response-time data, patrol coverage metrics, service call efficiency, and crime statistics before and after the facility becomes operational.

3503.description: The funds will support Keys AHEC's pediatric medical and dental program to deliver cost-effective restorative and primary care for children. By reducing emergency visits, preventing advanced disease, and improving long-term health outcomes, the program maximizes state investment while lowering future healthcare costs and strengthening community health infrastructure.
3503.purpose: Requested funds will support the Keys AHEC’s school-based medical and dental care program, enabling over 10,000+ medical/dental visits for primary medical care and restorative dental treatments. This will equate to approximately over 50,000 services to be provided in a cost efficient manner for children of working class and low income families in FY26–27.
3503.activities: The program will deliver pediatric restorative dental care, primary medical care, and acute care visits for children. Services include oral health exams, treatment of acute needs, and direct medical care for children. Mobile and clinic- based visits will provide access, increase patient encounters, and ensure care is delivered at school based care sites.
3503.direct_services: The funds will provide children with direct medical and dental services, including restorative care, physical exams, acute care and oral treatment. Services will be delivered in clinics and through mobile dental units and school based health clinics for working class and low income families improving long-term health outcomes.
3503.population: Keys AHEC serves uninsured, low income, and Medicaid-enrolled children across Monroe County, providing over 6,000 medical visits and 4,500 dental visits totaling 50,000+ services annually. Services are provided over 10 school based clinics, a centralized dental center and through a mobile dental unit that rotates to all public school locations.
3503.outcome: The project will improve children’s health and school attendance by providing preventive, restorative, and primary care services through school-based medical and dental clinics. Measurable results include fewer untreated illnesses and dental emergencies, reduced health-related absences, and earlier detection of chronic conditions. Success will be tracked through electronic health records (EHR) using CPT/ICD-10 codes, patient counts, and service data, and emergency referral rates.

3345.description: Funds needed to replace and improve the deteriorated Indian Prairie Boat Ramp with a modern, safe, and durable facility that ensures reliable public access to Lake Okeechobee. The ramp is a critical access point for recreation, fishing, hunting, camping, and watersports, as well as for emergency rescue operations and agency management of the lake that is used regularly by SFWMD, FWC and USACE. Improvements will include design, permitting, and construction of a new ramp, parking, and associated infrastructure. The project supports tourism, protects the environment by reducing unauthorized shoreline launches, and enhances safety for residents and visitors in this Rural Area of Opportunity.
3345.purpose: Goal is to replace the dangerous, failing Indian Prairie Boat Ramp with a modernized, safe, and environmentally responsible facility. The project will ensure continued public access to Lake Okeechobee for recreational, cultural, and tourism activities while providing a critical launch point for emergency response and agency management that is regularly used by SFWMD, USACE & Fish & Wildlife. Improves the quality of life, health and safety, protection of property and the environment.
3345.activities: To seek contractual services through the County's procurement policies and procedures for engineering, design, permitting, project management/administration, engineering during construction, on-site construction and construction of a new concrete boat ramp, parking facilities, and associated infrastructure. Improvements will reduce erosion and sediment runoff, expand safe access for boaters, and provide durable modern facilities that meet current safety and environmental standards.
3345.direct_services: Citizens will directly benefit through improved, safe recreational access for boating, fishing, hunting, and camping and outdoor recreational opportunities with direct access to Lake Okeechobee. The facility serves as an essential staging site for emergency response operations and lake management by agencies such as FWC, SFWMD, and USACE.
3345.population: Target population is the State, citizens, visitors, general public, Glades County, which is designated as a Rural Area of Opportunity. This popular and only boat ramp that provides direct access to Lake Okeechobee serves not only Glades County, the surrounding areas and out-of-state visitors for outdoor recreation is also heavily used by commercial fishing guides and State & Federal agencies (FWC/SFWMD/US Army Corp) conducting lake management and rescue operations.
3345.outcome: The expected outcomes include safer and more reliable public access to Lake Okeechobee, preservation of cultural and recreational traditions, improved water quality/quantity through erosion control, and increased economic activity from tourism. Quality, safe boating infrastructure supports tourism & economic activities that preserves long-term outdoor recreational access and community use of a historically important canal system. A new developer is coming to the area and is looking to promote Glades County as a regional fishing destination that will bring new visitors and professional fishing anglers to this Rural of Area of Opportunity. Outcomes measured by tracking construction completion,

3287.description: The requested funds are essential for the complete replacement of the West Glades Campus roofing system and critical flat roof repairs at Moore Haven Middle High School. This vital work will prevent immediate and long-term facility failures and directly serve the approximately 1,100 students, faculty, and staff across both campuses. By mitigating the severe health and safety risks from chronic water intrusion, we will strengthen the structural integrity of the buildings and significantly extend their lifespan
